enrich.summary_1line: Vercel's AI SDK 7 post describes agent features for developing, running, integrating harnesses, observing, and building beyond text.

text: AI SDK, with over 16 million weekly downloads, is the TypeScript SDK for building AI applications, features, frameworks, and agents across any model provider. It's the same layer eve , Vercel's open-source agent framework, is built on. AI SDK 7 adds production depth for agent work across five areas: Develop agents with reasoning control, tool and runtime context, provider files and skills support, MCP Apps, and a terminal UI. Run agents with tool approvals, durability ( WorkflowAgent ), timeouts, and sandbox support. Integrate any agent harness, such as Codex, Claude Code, Deep Agents, OpenCode, or Pi. Observe agents with telemetry, Node.js tracing channel, lifecycle events, and performance statistics. Go beyond text agents with provider-agnostic real-time voice support and video generation. Develop agents Building well-behaved agents requires fine-grained control over model reasoning, tool context, and file handling. Reasoning control Most frontier models support configurable reasoning, but every provider API exposes it differently. AI SDK 7 standardizes this with a reasoning option for generateText and streamText . It maps to provider-native reasoning settings, letting you control reasoning effort in a single line. You can also still fall back to provider options when you need more detailed provider-specific reasoning configuration. Learn more in the reasoning documentation . Tool context Tools are increasingly developed independently of specific agents or applications. For example, third-party companies offer tools that enable agents to use their APIs. Therefore, tools require additional inputs that are not generated by LLMs, such as API keys or configuration settings. AI SDK 7 adds a fully typed tool context that can be specified for each tool via a schema. The context is limited to the tool to prevent 3rd-party tools from accessing context they do not need. Learn more about Tool Context Runtime context For more complex agentic loops, you often need variables that you can access and modify in prepareStep to adjust prompts, model selection, and more. AI SDK 7 introduces a typed runtime context available during step preparation and tool approval functions, with optional telemetry support. This enables you to encapsulate more logic in ToolLoopAgent and share those agents with that internal logic. Learn more about Runtime Context . Provider file uploads Many agent workflows require handling large inputs, such as PDFs, images, datasets, or other artifacts. Sending those files inline is slow and wasteful, especially for stateless inference, where they get sent over and over again. AI SDK 7 adds a top-level uploadFile API that lets you upload a file once and then pass a lightweight reference into subsequent model calls. This avoids re-uploading the same bytes repeatedly, making inference faster and saving bandwidth during repeated or multi-step runs. uploadFile can be used with any providers that offer a file uploading endpoint. The function returns a provider reference object that is portable across providers. Learn more about Provider File Uploads Provider skill uploads Sending skills inline on every request to provider-managed container environments has the same overhead problem as sending files inline. AI SDK 7 adds a top-level uploadSkill API that lets you upload a skill once and then use a reference to it in subsequent inference calls. Similar to uploadFile , the function returns a provider reference object. Learn more about Provider Skill Uploads . MCP Apps MCP has become a common way to connect agents to tools and resources. But not every tool should be model-visible, and some MCP servers need to expose specialized UI alongside their tools. AI SDK 7 adds support for MCP Apps. MCP servers can now separate model-visible tools from app-only tools, preserve app metadata, and render app UIs inside sandboxed iframes. A JSON-RPC bridge connects tools, resources, and display interactions. This lets you build richer agent experien
title: AI SDK 7

enrich.summary_1line: AI SDK 7 is released with breaking requirements of Node.js 22 minimum and ESM imports, plus new agent, media, and realtime APIs.

text: AI SDK 7 is a major release for building production agents in TypeScript. The SDK has grown from model calls and chat primitives into a broader agent platform for developing, running, integrating, and observing agents across text, audio, realtime, image, and video. Every major provider is supported out of the box. At a Glance Develop agents with reasoning control, tool and runtime context, provider files and skills support, MCP Apps, and a terminal UI. Run agents with tool approvals, durable WorkflowAgent execution, first-class timeouts, and sandbox support. Integrate any agent harness such as Codex, Claude Code, Deep Agents, OpenCode, or Pi. Observe agent behavior with redesigned telemetry, @ai-sdk/otel , Node.js tracing channel support, lifecycle callbacks, and step performance statistics. Build beyond text with stable speech/transcription APIs, richer file parts, image generation and editing, multimodal embeddings, reranking, realtime voice (experimental), and video generation (experimental). Upgrade with clearer APIs through the new migration skill, codemods, and migration paths for ESM, Node.js 22, instructions , telemetry , stream , finalStep , runtimeContext , and toolsContext . Before You Upgrade AI SDK 7 introduces two breaking requirements: Node.js 22 minimum : Node 22 is required because the SDK depends on APIs (including the native fetch implementation and improved AsyncLocalStorage semantics) that are not backported to earlier LTS lines. ESM imports required : AI SDK 7 requires ESM imports ( import syntax or .mjs files). CommonJS require() is not supported. Update your package.json to include "type": "module" or migrate individual files to .mjs . Run the v7 codemods to automate most import and rename changes before manually reviewing semantic migration items. See the full v7 migration guide . Develop Agents Provider-agnostic reasoning control : generateText and streamText now support a top-level reasoning option that maps to provider-native settings across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, xAI, Bedrock, Fireworks, DeepSeek, Open Responses, and OpenAI-compatible providers. Note that exact behavior and available parameters vary by provider. Typed runtime context : Shared orchestration state lives in runtimeContext and flows through prepareStep , approval functions, lifecycle callbacks, telemetry, ToolLoopAgent , and WorkflowAgent . Scoped tool context : Tools can declare a contextSchema , and callers provide per-tool values through toolsContext , so third-party tools only receive the secrets or config they need. Provider file uploads : uploadFile uploads large inputs once and reuses provider references in later calls, reducing redundant uploads in repeated PDF, dataset, image, and multi-step workflows. Provider skill uploads : uploadSkill brings the same pattern to provider-managed skill environments. MCP Apps : MCP support now includes model-visible versus app-only tools, app metadata, sandboxed iframe rendering, and JSON-RPC communication for tools, resources, logs, and display updates. Add an MCP app to your agentic app. Terminal agent development : @ai-sdk/tui runs AI SDK agents in an interactive terminal UI, letting you test reasoning, tools, and markdown output before building a full app. Learn how to build your own terminal agent . Run Agents in Production AI SDK 7 adds the primitives agents need once they leave local demos. Tool approvals : generateText , streamText , and ToolLoopAgent can define approval policies at the call or agent level. Policies can require user approval, auto-approve, auto-deny, or delegate to typed approval functions. Hardened approval replay : Higher-risk approval flows can revalidate tool inputs and policies before continuation, use WorkflowAgent approval validation, and opt into HMAC signing. HMAC signing cryptographically binds the original tool inputs to the approval token, preventing tampering with tool arguments between the approval request and resumption. Durable execution : @a

text: AI costs are getting harder to forecast. As teams lean more on coding agents and other token-heavy workflows, a key can burn cost faster than anyone notices: Autonomous workflows that can loop or fan out without supervision Demos and prototypes that could catch unexpected traffic if shared or shipped Developers exploring or experimenting without a sense of per-model cost Set a spend cap on any key, and AI Gateway rejects further requests on that key once the limit is exceeded, until the budget resets or you raise it. Keys created programmatically will also appear in your team AI Gateway API Keys view , so you can see all keys in one place. Read the API keys documentation for more information about setting and using budgets for API keys. Read more

enrich.summary_1line: Vercel published an advisory for CVE-2026-23869, a high-severity React Server Components denial-of-service issue requiring upgrades.

text: Summary A high-severity vulnerability (CVSS 7.5) in React Server Components can lead to Denial of Service. We created new rules to address these vulnerabilities and deployed them to the Vercel WAF to automatically protect all projects hosted on Vercel at no cost. However, do not rely on the WAF for full protection. Immediate upgrades to a patched version are required. Impact A specially crafted HTTP request can be sent to any App Router Server Function endpoint that, when deserialized, may trigger excessive CPU usage. This can result in denial of service in unpatched environments. These vulnerabilities are present in Next.js 13.x, 14.x, 15.x, 16.x and affected packages using the App Router. The issue is tracked upstream as CVE-2026-23869 Resolution After creating mitigations to address this vulnerability, we deployed them across our globally-distributed platform to protect our customers. We still recommend upgrading to the latest patched version. Updated releases of React and affected downstream frameworks include fixes to prevent this issue. All users should upgrade to a patched version as soon as possible. Fixed In = 15.0.0 to be fixed in 15.5.15 = 16.0.0 to be fixed in 16.2.3 Read more
title: Summary of CVE-2026-23869

enrich.summary_1line: Stripe is now generally available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0, with live-account connection and automatic environment variable provisioning.

text: Building commerce applications looks very different than it did even a few years months ago. Teams are no longer treating storefronts and billing systems as long-running integration projects that happen after the product is complete. They iterate quickly, deploy globally by default, and increasingly rely on AI tools to generate UI, checkout flows, and subscription logic. Commerce is becoming more programmable and increasingly agent-driven. As AI systems begin to generate storefronts, assemble checkout flows, and optimize billing logic, the setup, integrations, and infrastructure need to be just as composable and automated. With tools like v0, and agentic coding agents working with Vercel CLI and Vercel Marketplace , developers can move from idea to deployed product much faster than before. As that workflow becomes more automated and AI-native, the surrounding systems need to keep pace, and the developer's experience (which includes the agent's) needs as much focus as the end-user's. An improved developer experience Historically, moving from a Stripe Sandbox to accepting live payments required retrieving API keys, copying them into environment variables, and verifying configuration across multiple environments. It worked, but it introduced unnecessary friction and risk at precisely the moment a team was ready to go live. Stripe is now generally available on the Vercel Marketplace and in v0 , with full support for connecting production accounts. You can connect an existing live Stripe account directly to a Vercel project or import one into your environment and begin accepting real payments without rebuilding your integration. The connection flow provisions the required environment variables automatically, so moving from test mode to live transactions does not require manual key exchange or rewiring your application. The beta release supported Stripe Sandbox account creation, and now general availability unlocks full production use cases, including live ecommerce storefronts, SaaS subscriptions, usage-based billing, and invoicing. With this release, going to production with payments is a single integration between your project and Stripe, rather than a separate configuration step that happens outside of it. Reducing setup friction while improving security Making payments easier to connect is only useful if it is also secure by default. To support production connections, Vercel partnered with Stripe to build a new set of key management APIs. Credentials are now generated, exchanged, and stored programmatically, reducing the surface area for human error while maintaining correct separation across development, preview, and production environments. Under the hood, the integration performs a cryptographic key exchange rather than requiring developers to manually retrieve and paste API credentials. The required Stripe keys are provisioned automatically and stored as environment variables within the appropriate Vercel environment, Stripe provides two types of API keys: Secret keys ( STRIPE_SECRET_KEY ): These must only be used in server-side code, such as API routes or Server Actions. They should never be exposed in client-side code or committed to version control Publishable keys ( NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY ): These are safe for client-side use. They identify your Stripe account but cannot perform sensitive operations. Get started With Stripe connected through the Vercel Marketplace, moving from a working application to live revenue becomes part of the same workflow you use to build and deploy your product. You can start with a simple example that creates a Checkout Session and deploy your first online store using Vercel and Stripe. Create a Checkout Session: Install Stripe from the Vercel Marketplace or v0 , connect your account, and your environment variables are ready before you write a line of payment code. See the changelog and documentation for more details. Read more
title: From idea to secure checkout in minutes with Stripe

enrich.summary_1line: Vercel Functions on Fluid Compute now use Active CPU pricing, at $0.128 per hour for active CPU and $0.0106 per GB-hour for provisioned memory.

text: Vercel Functions on Fluid Compute now use Active CPU pricing, which charges for CPU only while it is actively doing work. This eliminates costs during idle time and reduces spend for workloads like LLM inference, long-running AI agents, or any task with idle time. Active CPU pricing is built on three core metrics: Active CPU : Time your code is actively executing in an instance. Priced at $0.128 per hour Provisioned Memory: Memory allocated to the instance, billed at a lower rate. Priced at $0.0106 per GB-Hour Invocations : One charge per function call An example of this in action: A function running Standard machine size at 100% active CPU would now cost ~$0.149 per hour (1 Active CPU hour + 2 GB of provisioned memory). Previously this would have cost $0.31842 per hour (1.7 GB Memory × $0.18). Active CPU pricing is now enabled by default for all Hobby, Pro, and new Enterprise teams. For existing Enterprise customers, availability depends on your current plan configuration. This change takes effect after a redeploy. Learn more about Fluid compute with Active CPU pricing and read the announcement . Read more

text: Note: This post is historical and describes Edge Functions as they existed at the time. For new projects, use Vercel Functions with the Node.js runtime and Fluid compute . The field of artificial intelligence continues to take the world by storm. Huge strides have been made in text and image generation through tools like ChatGPT, GPT-3, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion. It’s spawned a wave of exciting AI startups, many of which we’re seeing built with Vercel and Next.js . One of the most exciting developments in the AI space is GPT-3, a cutting-edge natural language processing model developed by OpenAI . With its ability to understand and generate human-like text, GPT-3 has the potential to disrupt how we perform many of our tasks. This historical walkthrough uses twitterbio.com to show how streaming changed the user experience for GPT-3 apps. For new projects, build this pattern with Vercel Functions , Fluid compute , and streaming responses. The frontend The Next.js frontend consists of a few elements: A text box for users to copy their current bio or write a few sentences about themselves A dropdown where they can select the tone of the bio they want to be generated A submit button for generating their bio, which when clicked calls an API route that uses OpenAI’s GPT-3 model and returns two generated bios Two containers to display the generated bios after we get them back from the API route Here’s what the code for our index page looks like. We have a few pieces of state that correspond to the elements mentioned above. We’re also defining a prompt—like ChatGPT, we need to send a prompt to GPT-3 to instruct it to generate the new bios. Finally, we ask GPT-3 to generate two bios clearly labeled (so we can parse them correctly) using the user-provided bio and vibe as context. The rest of our index page is comprised of the UI elements themselves: our text box, dropdown, submit button, and two containers on the bottom that we display when we get the generated bios. There's also some loading logic for the button to show a loading indicator when clicked. In addition to the UI elements and the loading logic, we have a generateBio function that’s called when the user clicks the submit button. This sends a POST request to our /api/generate API route with the prompt in the body. We get the generated bios back from the API route, save it to the generatedBios state, then display it to the user. Because we asked GPT-3 to return the text in a specific numbered format, we can split it based on the “2.” to show the user the two bios separated nicely into containers as seen below. The backend A great advantage of using Next.js is being able to handle both our frontend and backend in a single application. We can spin up an API route just by creating a file called generate.ts in our api folder. Let’s take a look at our /api/generate API Route. We get the prompt from the request body that’s passed in on the frontend, then construct a payload to send to OpenAI. In this payload, we specify some important information like the exact model (GPT-3) and how many tokens we want OpenAI to respond with (a token is approximately 4 characters). In this case, we’re limiting the max tokens because Twitter bios have a character constraint. After the payload is constructed, we send it in a POST request to OpenAI, await the result to get back the generated bios, then send them back to the client as JSON. There we have it! We built the first version of our application. Feel free to check out the code and demo for this approach. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare post argues hosted AI agents obscure users from websites and proposes identity, reputation, and accountability mechanisms.

text:
AI agents act for millions, but servers see intermediaries that strip user visibility. This post defines the problem space and introduces a collaborative approach to safely identifying, allowing, and managing this automated traffic.

AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries. An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle: The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd. The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and
title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)

enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare launched analytics and per-agent access policies for personal AI agents visiting websites, with Allow, Block on pages with ads, or Block options.

text:
Personal AI agents have changed how users interact with the web, blurring the lines between automated and human traffic. Learn how Cloudflare gives site owners visibility and control to manage personal agent access.

Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time. In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use. For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants. Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it. Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block. We introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies. In Security Settings, you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block), Block on pages with ads, or Block. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available to all customers with Cloudflare One connectivity.

label.reason: Cloudflare private origins GA; mentions MCP servers and agent backends but mainly networking product news.

text:
Public traffic to private origins, with WAF, bot management, caching, and Workers, is now available to every customer with Cloudflare One connectivity.

Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group. Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins: Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations. Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN, no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh, a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins. Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually. The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network. The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error. For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record. POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true } Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path: { "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true } The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh. The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 Internet disruptions in Q3 2026, led by government-directed shutdowns and power outages.

label.reason: Quarterly internet outage review; general infrastructure interest, not his focus.

text:
An examination of global Internet disruptions observed by Cloudflare Radar during the third quarter of 2026. This review analyzes how power failures, natural disasters, and government shutdowns impacted network connectivity and traffic.

The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event. In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters. Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq, while renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region showed how quickly connectivity can become part of a broader political and humanitarian crisis. Outages within the United States, Japan, and Portugal — countries with a relatively strong history of Internet resilience — remind us that no country is immune to disruption. In total, Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 disruptions during the quarter. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 incidents, including 18 exam shutdowns in Iraq. Power outages followed with 14 incidents, while natural disasters accounted for five. The Internet is designed to be distributed and resilient, but that resilience still depends on electricity. When power fails, routers, mobile base stations, data centers, interconnection facilities, and the networks that connect them can fail with it. Over the past three months, that dependency was one of the clearest patterns in Radar’s disruption data. Power outages were the second-most common cause of disruptions by incident count this quarter, behind government-directed exam shutdowns. In Cuba, Internet disruptions followed the erratic patterns of an unstable power grid. Radar observed four power-related outages across the quarter, meaning connectivity was affected by grid failures at least once a month. The outages took place July 6, July 14, August 3, and a three-day blackout from September 18 to 20. The traffic volume decreases ranged from 18% on July 14 to 59% on August 3. Honduras illustrated how a localized infrastructure failure can produce national-level effects. A power failure on September 10 at an interconnection facility affected at least 11 major providers, showing how concentrated traffic exchange points can become single points of failure. The outage lasted approximately three hours, during which HTTP traffic across the country fell by 63%. Two notable exceptions were the cross-border provider Telecomunicaciones de Guatemala (AS14754) and mobile carrier Celtel (AS52262), which were unaffected. This suggests that their Honduran connectivity may rely more heavily on infrastructure outside the country. On July 5, a power outage in Sevastopol, Ukraine, caused an eight-hour blackout, with HTTP traffic dropping by 98%. A little over a month later, on August 12, drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure caused another power outage, resulting in a ten-hour Internet disruption and up to a 95% decline in traffic volume. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare reports SGLang bug exposed cross-request KV cache data in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI from August 27 to September 9, 2026.

label.reason: Real KV cache cross-tenant leak in SGLang serving of GLM-5.3; inference serving and AI security lessons.

text:
A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.

On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions. After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it: To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid requ
title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang

enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare releases Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans that serves byte-range requests using chunk-aligned caching.

label.reason: Pingora range-request caching redesign; distributed systems interest but CDN-specific, not AI.

text:
Naive byte-range caching can waste gigabytes of origin bandwidth on small requests. We rebuilt our cache architecture in Pingora to coordinate partial fetches automatically, cutting R2 p99 latency in half.

A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule, and Cloudflare handles the rest. An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range: HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576 Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it. The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it. Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration. The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post: each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone. The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key. This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming, a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range. The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology. Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently. Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora-based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers. The fix came from something Pingora was already d
title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning

enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare launches PQ GeoKey Manager in closed beta, restricting where post-quantum-protected customer private keys can be unwrapped.

label.reason: Post-quantum geo-fenced key management closed beta; niche crypto product.

text:
Cloudflare's new post-quantum GeoKey Manager protects geographically fenced decryption keys from harvest now, decrypt later attacks. Learn how we redesigned our cryptography stack to support strict data sovereignty in a post-quantum world.

Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography. While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography. Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later. For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work. Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security (TLS) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager. This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network. GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key. That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel. This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries. In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used fr
title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management

enrich.summary_1line: Commerce.com enables WebMCP across almost 100,000 storefront domains on Cloudflare, with a per-merchant edge opt-out.

label.reason: WebMCP for agent shopping across 100k stores; relevant to MCP and agent tooling.

text:
Almost 100,000 Commerce.com domains now give AI agents real shopping tools through WebMCP on Cloudflare. Here's how we turned it on across every store at once, while keeping each merchant in control.

AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online. That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it. Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products. Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf. In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCP in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code. Commerce.com, a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked: Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once? Here’s why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way. Kristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts: “Merchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesn’t have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchant’s site, and the merchant keeps the relationship. We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. That’s where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly. WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side MCP, and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopper’s browser. It’s the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants don’t have to choose between the two or manage them separately.” Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.com’s backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic. When visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP. Suppose you tell your agent: "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart." title: How Commerce.com and Cloudflare are getting storefronts ready for AI agents

enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare reports eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised; Cloudflare released mitigations and client updates.

label.reason: Compromised eMudhra (Indian CA) certificates enabling forged certs; serious security incident, India-linked, affects developers.

text:
Following the discovery that eight eMudhra intermediate certificates use weak keys, Cloudflare is deploying mitigations and releasing client updates. We explain the impact, our response, and what customers and developers should do next.

On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet. We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services. We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected. We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms. Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below. For developers, look beneath the SDK. An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy. Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore. This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment. Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier. The timeline of events so far is below. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare reports cutting its AI code reviewer's average cost per review by 68%, to $0.77, via prompt caching and model changes.

label.reason: Concrete AI code reviewer inference cost cut 68% via prompt caching and model routing; directly production LLM engineering.

text:
When our AI code reviewer's cost per run doubled, we dug into the token usage to find out why. Learn how we used prompt caching and intelligent model routing to slash our inference bill by 68% while speeding up reviews.

When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April, an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave. Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before. About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in. The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data. The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though. At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models. Our internal standards reviewer, Codex, ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself. The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost. One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable. We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out! Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again. That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it. I know where the shops are. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Louis The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker. text:
Today, we laid out our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world. The post GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe, we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: GitHub is built for developers and their agents. We’re also making the underlying primitives available, so you can build your own bespoke solutions. You stay in control of the work, the tools, and the cost. Today at Universe, we showed some of the latest products and features in action, starting with the GitHub Copilot app. The GitHub Copilot app is designed from the ground up for agentic software delivery. It connects your agents and tools across projects, so you can direct the work without making every handoff. And it’s for more than producing code: you can write specs, present design discussions, or analyze telemetry in one agent-first surface. Different tasks need different models. text:
We moved a copy of 99.99999% of GitHub's repositories to Azure. Here's how per-reference quorums will bring over the rest, and how object storage lets reads scale independently. The post The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the architecture once it arrived. Git operations are a Tier 0 service: they’re a core function of GitHub, and nearly everything in GitHub depends on the repository data. That meant the data, services, and every dependency had to move first. The first copy of a repository landed in Azure’s Central US region in August 2025. Today, most repositories have two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. For most of that time, Azure absorbed our growth while our own data centers held steady. During the migration, traffic follows the data. Most repositories have five replicas to balance durability, availability, and scale. To minimize read latency, Spokes uses preferential routing to direct traffic to a replica in the same region and availability zone as the request. As replicas move to Azure, the share of the traffic that can be served from Azure grows with each one, until the last replica arrives and the old region stops receiving requests entirely. Every repository goes through this process: So, what about the remaining 0.00001% of repositories? In our current architecture, a repository hosted in more than one region has a lower write throughput ceiling. Spokes’ quorum only needs a majority to commit a write, but it waits for every healthy replica to respond (up to a timeout) before moving on, so slow replicas delay every write rather than falling behind. In practice, that means the slowest healthy replica sets the latency of every write, and because each write holds a repository-wide lock until it commits, it also sets the throughput ceiling. Once a replica lives in the target Azure region, it’s about 1,000 miles from our data centers, making each network round trip around 25ms, and a write requires multiple round trips. A repository already near its throughput ceiling can’t absorb that on every serialized write; it would fall further behind with every push. This is where our first principle, minimizing coordination, comes into play. Specifically for this case: don’t serialize what doesn’t need to be. Git’s consistency requirements apply to each reference individually. Once the server accepts an update to a reference, no client should see an older value afterward, only that value or a newer one. enrich.summary_1line: Kubernetes announces a Workload Conformance Working Group to write a shared specification and tests for runtime workload behavior.

label.reason: Kubernetes working group announcement on workload conformance standard; niche, early-stage.

text: We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group . The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version . Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions . Even so, every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support. A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from. What the working group will deliver The charter sets out three deliverables: A specification of workload behavior for each Kubernetes minor version. A method for testing each requirement against a running workload. Upstream conformance tooling that implements those tests. The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers. The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn't yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification. The specification covers how a workload runs, and importantly not what it does. Consequently, application logic is out of scope of workload conformance. The binary won't retest anything Certified Kubernetes already covers, and it won't require a particular workload packaging format, or vendor tool like policy engine, security scanner, etc. How the work is organized Two Special Interest Groups (SIGs) are sponsors for the working group. SIG Architecture will own the specification and tooling through a subproject, which will be created once the first artifacts are proposed by the Working Group. SIG Apps will bring the application perspective. Whenever a requirement touches another Kubernetes SIG's area, such as node behavior or networking, the working group will initiate conversations with those SIGs as well. The working group is a forum where SIGs can get involved and shape the direction of Workload Conformance while the specification is being written. We're aiming for a stable first specification and working tests within two to three Kubernetes release cycles. Get involved The specification will and needs to be built from real examples, so we want to hear your experiences. If you run clusters, tell us how you assess workloads today and what broke during your last upgrade or maintenance window. If you maintain an application, tell us what it needs from the cluster and where the existing guidance left you guessing. Beyond examples, the work needs reviewers for proposed requirements and contributors to write the tests and tooling. When early versions of the tests are ready, we also want early testers to run the binary against your own workloads and tell us where the results differ between runs or environments. enrich.summary_1line: Kubernetes v1.37 promotes HPA scale-to-zero to Beta and enables it by default, allowing workloads to scale to zero replicas using object or external metrics.

text: Kubernetes v1.37 includes API support for horizontal autoscaling of workloads down to zero replicas. This feature is now Beta and enabled by default. A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) that uses a suitable object metric or external metric can now scale a workload to zero replicas, then bring it back when the metric changes. Before v1.37, you needed an add-on or external component, or you had to enable the Alpha feature gate, to scale from zero. It is now part of core Kubernetes. Scaling to zero removes the last idle Pod from workloads such as queue consumers and batch processors. The savings are largest when each Pod reserves expensive resources, including dedicated CPUs or GPUs. The trade-off is cold-start time: the HPA must observe the metric, schedule a Pod, and start the application. This works well when work can wait in a durable queue. Kubernetes Services do not buffer requests while no Pods are ready, so HTTP and other request-driven workloads need a separate buffering layer. Why scaling from zero needs a different metric The HPA commonly scales on CPU or memory usage. Both metrics come from running Pods. Once the replica count reaches zero, there are no Pods left to measure and no signal that can tell the HPA to scale back up. Object and external metrics do not have that limitation. A queue length, for example, exists independently of the workers that consume it. The HPA can continue reading the queue length while no workers are running. The following example scales a queue consumer to and from zero using an external metric. Configure an external metric The following example uses a Prometheus metric named queue_consumer_lag . It assumes that Prometheus already collects a series similar to this one: queue_consumer_lag { namespace = " default ", name = " worker_tasks "} Kubernetes needs a metrics adapter to make that value available through the External Metrics API. One implementation is the Prometheus Adapter , which can expose the series using an externalRules entry: externalRules : - seriesQuery : '{__name__="queue_consumer_lag",name!=""}' metricsQuery : sum(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}) by (name) resources : overrides : namespace : resource : namespace The exact adapter installation and discovery rules depend on your monitoring setup. See the Prometheus Adapter guide to external metrics for the full configuration options. Before creating the HPA, you can verify that Kubernetes can read the metric: kubectl get --raw \ '/apis/external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/queue_consumer_lag?labelSelector=name%3Dworker_tasks' The request should return the current value for worker_tasks . If it does not, fix the metrics pipeline before configuring the HPA. An HPA cannot scale from zero when its metric is unavailable. Configure the HPA The following HPA targets a Deployment named queue-worker . It allows between zero and ten replicas, with one replica requested for each 30 queued tasks: apiVersion : autoscaling/v2 kind : HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata : name : queue-worker annotations : kubernetes.io/description : "Scales queue-worker based on the number of queued tasks" spec : scaleTargetRef : apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : Deployment name : queue-worker minReplicas : 0 maxReplicas : 10 metrics : - type : External external : metric : name : queue_consumer_lag selector : matchLabels : name : worker_tasks target : type : Value value : "30" When the queue is empty, the HPA can reduce the Deployment to zero replicas. When tasks arrive, the external metric remains available and the HPA calculates a new replica count, capped at ten by maxReplicas . Start the Deployment with at least one replica. Manually setting a Deployment to zero has always paused autoscaling. The HPA preserves that behavior and will not wake a workload that it did not scale down itself. Normal HPA behavior still applies.
