enrich.summary_1line: Netflix describes Quasar, which indexes symbols across repositories so library producers can see which consumers use changed APIs.

label.reason: Netflix Java library change impact tooling; mentions coding agents but mainly Java platform engineering, off his stack.

text: By Roberto Perez Alcolea , Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves. Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next: Does any consumer still call this method? Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations? Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact? Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign? At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds. Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally. We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions: What changed in the library’s public API? Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed? The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing. From API Changes to Consumer Impact Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive. Quasar builds on SCIP , an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently. On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change. During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings
title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes

enrich.summary_1line: Netflix introduces single-tenant Titus, a mode giving selected tasks their own virtual machine while keeping the Titus API and managed experience.

label.reason: Kubernetes-based container platform on AWS with VM-level isolation; relevant devops/cloud and sandbox isolation topics.

text: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host. We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched. The cost of good neighbors Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management. These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota. A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota. We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised t

enrich.summary_1line: Netflix describes an Observability Ontology: a W3C-stack knowledge graph linking telemetry, alerting, incident and deployment systems to speed root-cause investigations.

text: Prasanna Vijayanathan , Renzo Sanchez-Silva When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded. This post is about that search for the needle. The Four hours before a fix Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it? As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner. The MELT Layer “What caused the issue?” Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to. MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system. The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer: What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves out The timeline of an investigation So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again? A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hours In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover. The disagreement underneath The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow. It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle. Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas , our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found. enrich.summary_1line: Netflix describes a low-rank choice model that estimates the causal effect of personalized recommendations, validated against randomized experiments.

label.reason: Recommender system causal measurement at Netflix; ML-adjacent but outside his focus.

text: By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan Kallus Introduction Personalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog. But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time? In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings. The Measurement Challenge A natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand. The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences. One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy. Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence. A Model of Member Choice To measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see. A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. text: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. text: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. text: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. text: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments. An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all. Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says. text:
A frontier benchmark spanning RSI, hardware design, cyber, bio, finance, legal, quant trading, chip design, software engineering, materials science, and alignment

GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities. We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI, not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. Specifically, we cover the following domains: Chip design Cybersecurity Biology Finance Legal Quant trading Recursive self-improvement (RSI) Hardware design Materials science Alignment Software engineering And intentionally forgo industries like government, real estate, and insurance. GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12%. It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead. We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available. We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin. We also generally observe meaningful spikiness across all leading models. Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0. Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes. The cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely. It’s impossible to make all the nuanced comparisons enabled by GDPx in a single newsletter. To explore the data yourself, checkout the official website. Domain-specific benchmarks have gotten significantly better over the past year largely thanks to the rise of specialized RL environment startups. The 2027 datacenter boom is already being built, and next week’s midterms won’t stop it now. Roughly three-quarters of the 33.8 GW due across our top 20 states is already under construction, which is why we remain comfortable with the global +50 GW year we laid out in our Oct. 16 article. The campuses are taking shape. The election will change the rules around them, but much of the 2027 pipeline already has a substantial head start. The fight is over 2028. Our model has 62.2 GW of US net additions that year, most of which hasn’t started construction. Much of it sits in states electing a governor on Nov. 3. This piece tracks the 13 states with the largest 2028 net additions in our model, setting aside Virginia and Mississippi, which don’t hold state elections this November. Together they account for 43.5 GW, or 70% of what we expect nationally, and 10 of the 13 elect a governor. Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model That leaves a 2028 pipeline still working through approvals, power projects, and construction schedules as the rules change. In September, we argued that datacenter moratoriums weren’t killing the US buildout: of roughly 20 GW inside local restrictions, we estimated only 1.5 GW faced delay. Most exposed capacity already had protections or did not need the affected approval until after the pause expired. That broad conclusion has held up. What is changing is the reach of the restrictions given the growing anti-datacenter backlash. Three things have worsened since. Texas, the largest US market, froze Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) permits on Sept. 21 on top of the interconnection-queue audit begun Aug. 3, bringing onsite power into the hold. Oregon expanded its earlier state-land freeze to air and water-discharge permits on Oct. 9, through July 1, 2027. And midterm candidates have campaigned on more restrictive positions: nine of the 20 nominees want a pause on new construction and the other 11 want conditions; the split is about even by party. Both parties want developers to accept stricter conditions. The main difference is whether a developer can meet the new terms and keep building or must wait for the state to reopen approvals. The biggest risk to our buildout forecast right now is a prolonged permitting freeze at the TCEQ. Texas alone adds close to 30% of US GW in 2028. A few months of lost time in that market can move the national number. We already flagged to Datacenter Model subscribers which companies are most at risk from the current pause. The question now is how long the pause lasts. Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who is running for re-election in Texas, could reopen permitting once the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the state’s grid operator, finishes its audit and the Texas Water Development Board completes its water-use review. ERCOT is targeting Dec. 10 to file its report, which does not by itself reopen permitting. A restart around then would leave developers dealing with a relatively short interruption, which some projects can absorb within their schedules. The audit still has to lead to a decision to resume issuance, and each permit still needs approval. By contrast, Gina Hinojosa (D), his challenger, presents a more bearish approach: she would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for datacenters. The regular legislative session in Texas takes place from Jan. 12 to May 31, 2027. If approvals stay on hold throughout that session, the freeze would last about eight months from September. If reopening waits for the new rules to take effect in late summer, the freeze would last close to a year, or five to nine additional months compared with restarting in December. text: AI safety is on fire. On 12 September 2026, Dario Amodei published an essay arguing that frontier labs must deliberately slow the pace at which they improve model capabilities. China was central to his geopolitical argument: export controls and tighter security could preserve America’s lead, creating room to slow down and leverage for a future agreement with Beijing. Within a day, Sam Altman and Elon Musk supported Dario’s call. However, President Trump scoffed. On 14 September 2026, he wrote that fears of AI destroying humanity are “a HOAX” and that “the only one that is happy about it is China.” Beijing scoffed too, with the state-run Global Times calling Dario’s essay a “Cold War playbook.” The debate then moved onto the diplomatic calendar. On 20 September 2026, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first US-China AI dialogue. On 23 September 2026, President Xi Jinping began his state visit to the US. The Trump-Xi summit formalized the dialogue as the “US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue,” using the name Trump had unveiled at the UN the day before Xi arrived. The summit also promised a channel for AI incidents. On 29 September 2026, Trump and six executives signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a one-page voluntary pledge to self-police that Trump called “morally binding.” China sits on both sides of the American argument. For President Trump, competition with China is a reason not to slow down. For Dario, preserving America’s lead over China is what makes slowing down possible. Nobody has asked what China is actually doing. So, we did. What do the Chinese government, frontier labs, and AI experts say and do about AI safety? And what should American labs, investors, and policymakers conclude from it? Beijing’s stated position is the most safety-forward of any major AI power outside Europe. Xi Jinping told the Politburo in April 2025 that AI brings “unprecedented risks and challenges” and ordered systems for technical monitoring, risk early-warning and emergency response. At the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, Xi said the world must “ensure AI always remains under human control” and that the faster AI advances, “the more promptly the measures to prevent loss of control must be improved.” China signed the Bletchley Declaration and the Paris and New Delhi statements, co-sponsored the UN resolutions, founded a World AI Cooperation Organization in Shanghai, and publishes bilingual AI Safety Governance Frameworks. enrich.summary_1line: SemiAnalysis examines how sparse attention and KV cache offloading affect memory, and compares GLM-5.3 serving cost across GPU platforms.

label.reason: Sparse attention, KV cache offloading and HBM usage in GLM-5.3; directly about inference serving.

text:
GLM-5.3, KV Cache Offloading, HiSparse, DeepSeek Sparse Attention, IndexShare, Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization, Cybersecurity

How does sparse attention affect the TAM of memory, including HBM and NAND? Sparse attention selects top-k most relevant tokens to attend to, reducing the memory consumption and bandwidth requirements during the core Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA) operation. However, the efficiency improvement doesn’t directly translate to overall memory savings in practice. Concretely, the top-k selection operation typically requires the full context to be in HBM, so sparse attention doesn’t eliminate the memory capacity bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, the SGLang team designed HiSparse, a hierarchical memory system that proactively offloads KV cache entries from device HBM to host DRAM. HiSparse behaves like an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache, where it loads tokens from DRAM to HBM upon top-k selection cache miss, and it offloads tokens from HBM to DRAM based on the LRU eviction policy. To reduce the cache miss latency, HiSparse overlaps KV cache loading of layer N with the execution of layer N-1 (layer-wise overlapping), introduced in HiSparse’s prior work HiCache. Sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth requirements at the SDPA operation, but it does not reduce the overall memory capacity usage. In addition, HiSparse shows that system optimizations can overcome sparse attention’s memory capacity limitations, so sparse attention memory profile alone cannot sufficiently portray the full picture of system KV cache efficiency. Among the Dynamo-SGLang results, GB300 serves roughly 13950 total tokens per second per GPU here, a 17.5% throughput advantage versus 11873 total tokens for GB200. However, we assume $2.31 per GB300 GPU hour versus $1.86 for GB200. The higher hourly cost more than offsets GB300’s throughput lead at this target. In comparison with AMD, ATOM costs about 13% less than GB200 at 100 tokens per second. GB200 costs about 5% less at 125 and 12% less at 150. enrich.summary_1line: SemiAnalysis publishes a teardown of Intel Panther Lake, covering Intel 18A backside power delivery and comparisons with TSMC and Samsung nodes.

text:
Looking inside Intel 18A and Intel’s Panther Lake. A free SemiAnalysis STEEL teardown.

Panther Lake debuts the first commercial implementation of a backside power delivery network (BSPDN), introduces Intel’s first iteration of gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, and showcases their advanced packaging capabilities with its Foveros-S assembly. With Panther Lake, Intel’s manufacturing arc has shifted from nebulous roadmaps to shipped silicon, a significant milestone on their long road back to competitive semiconductor manufacturing. To evaluate the extent of Intel’s comeback, we tore down Panther Lake. The SemiAnalysis STEEL teardown lab breaks down advanced datacenter and AI hardware. To learn more about our pipeline or to commission a teardown, contact sales@semianalysis.com. WE’RE HIRING: Architecture, floorplan, packaging, manufacturing, and labs experts. Opportunities from system to transistor and everywhere in between. Check out our Careers page. Our teardown traces 18A from its four-sheet RibbonFETs (Intel’s marketing name for GAAFETs) and gate stacks through contacts, frontside and backside wiring, and the bonded carrier. We explain how these material and integration choices improve gate control and reduce resistance, while adding capacitance, thermal resistance, and process complexity. Our measurements put Panther Lake’s 18A compute logic and TSMC N3E GPU logic at similar logic density. However, 18A does not lead TSMC N3P, N2 or Samsung SF2 in peak density. Panther Lake’s CPU cores are incremental updates, and the high-end GPU still uses TSMC N3E. Panther Lake assembles one compute tile, one GPU tile, and one I/O tile atop a passive base tile using Intel’s Foveros-S advanced packaging. Both compute tile variants use Intel 18A. The Xe3 GPU options are a 4-core GT1 tile on Intel 3 and a larger 12-core GT2 tile on TSMC N3E. Both I/O tile variants use TSMC N6. [1], [2] Our analysis centers on the PTL-U compute tile, both the 4-core and 12-core GPU tiles, as well as the 12-lane I/O tile. In conventional chips, power and signal are routed through the same frontside metal stack towards the device frontend. Power rails consume scarce routing resources near the transistors, while tall via stacks carry VDD and VSS from the coarse upper wires to local rails. Backside power delivery network (BSPDN) moves the main power network behind the transistor layer, to the backside, separating it from frontside signal routing. We covered BSPDN and its impacts in 2024. [3], [4], [5] Intel’s BSPDN implementation, branded as “PowerVia”, routes power through dedicated backside metals to nano-TSVs, which connect those rails to local source/drain (S/D) contacts. Implementing that separation requires Intel to build the interconnect stacks from both sides of the wafer. The frontside comprises the M0-M14 signal stack, while the backside comprises the BM0-BM5 power stack. M0 and BM0 are closest to the transistors. The nano-TSVs connect the two sides, but Intel patterns and etches each via from the front after forming the contacts. A narrow via runs from the side of the contact deep into the silicon substrate. Intel then completes the frontside signal metal stack, bonds the wafer to a carrier, flips it and removes the original substrate until the buried via tips are exposed. The backside metal stack is then deposited directly on the revealed vias. The nano-TSV and backside-via profiles taper in opposite directions because Intel forms them from opposite sides of the wafer. The transistor structures form the FEOL. Local contacts and nano-TSVs connect them to the wiring. M0 begins the frontside interconnect stack. The silicon carrier remains attached above the frontside interconnects. It supports the device wafer during substrate removal and backside processing and remains part of the finished chip’s thermal path. text:
Jensen Sandbagging Performance Again, 2x more Annual Profit Per GigaWatt, The More you Buy, The More you Earn, AgentX, InferenceX, Extreme Co-Design

Rubin is the first platform co-designed across six products for the agentic era: Rubin GPU, Vera CPU, NVLink 6 Switch, ConnectX-9, BlueField-4, and Spectrum-6. Today we are publishing the first verified agentic inference results for Rubin, measured on our agentic inference benchmark, AgentX. Even on early pre-release software, the results already show why extreme co-design was necessary. At GTC 2026, Jensen presented this graph that VR NVL72 achieved 3x performance per MW compared to Blackwell on O(1-3 Trillion) parameter model around 200 TPS. But when compared to the real world performance of Rubin already on prelease software, we are already seeing up to 7x better token throughput per megawatt. Jensen needs to stop sandbagging his performance claims at GTC. The last time he did this at GTC 2024, when he claimed GB200 NVL72 would deliver 30x Hoppers performance, but when we tested, it was 98x better performance than Hopper. Our estimates on the performance results show that even on early software builds, Rubin can earn over 2x more profit per gigawatt than the Blackwell platform. As the Rubin software stack and kernel libraries mature, and as the developer community builds experience optimizing for Rubin, we expect that gap to widen further. We evaluate the performance using the industry standard agentic inference benchmark scenario called AgentX. This replays real world agentic traffic across our fleet of thousands of chips. The results can thus be holistically referenced by actual inference providers and hyperscale AI labs to decide which chips are most efficient in what scenarios. Our benchmark has been widely reproduced, validated and/or supported by almost every major buyer of compute from Google Cloud to Microsoft Azure to Oracle, to Meta and many more. Furthermore, it has the support of the ML community including from vLLM, LMCache, SGLang, PyTorch, Huggingface and the support of major labs like OpenAI, MiniMax, ZAI, Qwen, Moonshot Kimi, etc. Thank you to Jensen Huang, Ian Buck, Nick Comly, Kedar Potdar, Rohit Nagraj, and the Mainland China TensorRTLLM Team for helping on doing next gen Rubin software bring up and helping verify our agentic benchmark results. Star the InferenceX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful!. InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, NVIDIA, & AMD and soon SambaNova & Trainium. Due to how realistic AgentX scenario is to real world agentic inference workloads, AMD has committed to collaborating on MI455X UALoE72 too. At a high level, an agentic workload is characterized by four elements: Multi-turn: a session includes tens or hundreds of interactions between the user and assistant, compared with a handful in a chatbot scenario. These workloads combine long contexts and high prefill reuse with sub-agent bursts and numerous tool calls. Long context: system prompts, tool definitions, and the large number of turns make context accumulate quickly. High prefix reuse: since the conversation progresses linearly, where output from turn n-1 is concatenated to turn n (typically), most context can be served from KV cache rather than recomputed (this depends on the amount of storage available to store KV tensors). As n grows, the ratio of cached input relative to uncached typically tends towards 1. Sub-agent bursts: a session launches multiple short-lived sub-agents with fresh context, which create bursty KV-cache patterns. Read more about the methodology in our AgentX article. enrich.summary_1line: A decade-old OpenSSH and musl flaw lets attackers log into some Alpine Linux devices with no password.

text:
Certain configurations of Alpine are affected. Other distros may be as well.

Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password. The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations. There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices

enrich.summary_1line: Browser makers blocked eight intermediate TLS certificates from India-based eMudhra after weak private keys were found.

text:
Intermediate certs allow anyone to mint web credentials for any Internet server.

Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet. As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices. The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide.
title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs

Plex fixed four vulnerabilities at the start of last month. Three weeks later, published CVE designations revealed five vulnerabilities, with one of them carrying a severity rating of 8.6 out of 10. A researcher last week revealed an exploit that chained four of them together to achieve remote code execution of the device running a vulnerable Plex version. The researcher named the chain "Plex2Shell." The new details allowed a separate researcher to create a honeypot that could track attempts in the wild to exploit the vulnerability chain. Within a day, the researcher began seeing active scanning of the simulated Plex server and eventually successful attempts to infect devices. So far, successful attacks are installing two payloads. One is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet controlled by the attacker. The other payload is residential proxy software, which allows people to anonymize their Internet activity (much of it illegal) by connecting to the infected box and then using it to send the user’s traffic to a final destination.

enrich.summary_1line: Opposable, an MCP-compatible tool, lets AI agents tap, swipe, and type on Android phones and control iPhones through a companion computer.

label.reason: AI agent controlling phones via MCP client; snarky coverage of a thin product launch.

text:
Nothing will ruin your faith in humanity like an AI that operates your smartphone slowly, struggles with basic tasks, and can charge you for it

Why use your smartphone when AI can do it for you? We’ve reached a new level of AI inanity with the launch of Opposable, a tool that taps, swipes, and types on Android phones and controls iPhones through a companion computer, sparing users the apparent burden of operating their own devices. If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone. You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy. Lame. Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves. As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it. The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised). Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved. Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands. In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of two minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper. Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use. A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening the clock app and switching to the stopwatch tab takes it about 96 seconds, which is supposed to be impressive, apparently, as the company behind Opposable decided to showcase it on the thing’s website. As for Opposable’s ability to actually accomplish tasks, well, that’s not exactly a sure thing. “On eight tasks the model had never been tuned on, run on the emulator twice each, giving it the whole task succeeded 4 and 3 times,” the blog post notes. I’m pretty sure my brain and hands can do better without burning tokens to fail. “Giving it one subgoal at a time and checking each claimed success against the accessibility tree before the next subgoal succeeded 6 times in both rounds,” the blog continues - so even when it gets babysat each step of the way, it still only succeeds at three-quarters of tasks. Cool - that’s really going to free up all
title: Reach new heights of laziness by burning tokens to let an AI tap your smartphone screen for you

label.reason: KDE anniversary and AI-native desktop proposal; desktop Linux, not his focus.

text:
Akademy talk imagines Plasma assembling itself around a personal model of each user

KDE's annual conference takes place this weekend at Graz University of Technology in Austria, with an AI-native desktop proposal likely to divide attendees. The KDE project is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, giving delegates at the Akademy conference in Graz another reason to raise a glass. The conference begins on Saturday, September 19, and registration remains open. Although Xfce 1.0 appeared slightly earlier, its initial releases were proprietary, making what was originally known as the Kool Desktop Environment one of the earliest entirely FOSS desktop environments for Linux. Version 1.0 was released in July 1998. Although created for Linux, KDE software now runs on several other operating systems. The potentially contentious proposal comes in a Sunday afternoon talk entitled What would it take? A lovable, sovereign, AI-native KDE, presented by longtime KDE contributors Eva Brucherseifer and Jan Muehlig. In 2003, they conducted a usability study of the then newly released KDE 3.1. Of the 60 office workers tested, none of whom had prior Linux experience, 87 percent said they enjoyed working with KDE. The talk has three parts: what KDE learned – or failed to learn – from that study; the case for an "AI-native" desktop; and the importance of a sovereign European computing stack. It is the middle section that may ruffle feathers. The outline says: "A desktop that loves you back has to know you. Personal AI has crossed the threshold where the desktop itself can be compiled per user, per device, per moment, from a small portable model of the user – what we are sketching as Kadai: an encrypted, vendor-agnostic personal kernel from which Plasma assembles each Activity. "Plasma is uniquely well-fit for this – Activities, Plasmoids, the existing scripting surface – but a handful of upstream changes (declarative reconciliation, per-widget capabilities, richer Activity metadata) would turn KDE into the first shell that treats AI as infrastructure rather than as a chat box bolted to the side." This is very much not what this vulture wants from a desktop computer. It may win admirers, but seems more likely to polarize the audience. Writer and AI critic David Gerard points out the proposal's resemblance to the Resonant Computing Manifesto, launched in December 2025 at Wired's Big Interview in San Francisco. Gerard criticized the manifesto later that month. Gerard also notes that contributors to the Trinity Desktop Environment, a fork of KDE 3, have begun dabbling with AI-generated code – potentially disappointing those who viewed Trinity as an escape route. Anyone determined to keep AI off their desktop might instead check on the progress of the Sonic Desktop Environment, which we covered in July. ®
title: KDE turns 30 and someone's brought an AI-native desktop proposal

enrich.summary_1line: OpenClaw 2.0 prioritizes simpler installation and a redesigned browser interface, with security criticized as insufficient.

text:
Making installation easier and putting a new wrapper on the interface while leaving most of the security to users is a recipe for more trouble with the popular agent harness

OpenClaw has unveiled what its makers call its largest ever update – large enough to earn a 2.0 moniker – with usability taking center stage, along with some security updates that critics are suggesting will be insufficient. The OpenClaw foundation announced the release of version 2.0 of its AI agent harness on Sunday, describing it as something with far more scope than they ever intended it to have. “This update touches every part of OpenClaw,” Foundation community manager Hannes Rudolph said of the update. “We started by simplifying installation and rebuilding the browser app as a first-class experience, but doing that properly meant carrying the cleanup through the rest of OpenClaw until it became OpenClaw 2.0.” It's those two features – the rebuilt installation experience and redesigned interface – that Rudolph dedicates most of his announcement to. OpenClaw is an open-source, self-hosted AI agent harness that allows users to build their own AI agents and connect them to whatever apps and services they want. OpenClaw went viral shortly after its launch due to its extensive capabilities, and helped launch the AI agent craze. But, by empowering AI models with agentic capabilities, it exposed numerous security problems with unrestrained automation. In version 2.0, the new installation process is designed to be simpler, ostensibly to get more people using OpenClaw. “We cut or simplified a lot of configuration and moved the rest out of initial setup, letting people get to a first conversation faster and finish setting up their Claw by talking to it,” Rudolph explained. As for the user experience, Rudolph explained that the OpenClaw browser app has been redesigned into “a first-class experience” where users can continue setup and interact with their agent. “The web-based experience in OpenClaw now feels more familiar to anyone who uses apps like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity, with conversations in the sidebar and the one you are working in at the centre instead of opening on a separate Overview page,” the patch notes for the release explains. In other words, OpenClaw’s basic interface now looks just like the chat interface for every other AI service you’ve likely used on the web. The last major feature update added in OpenClaw 2.0 is shared cloud sessions. Per the announcement, OpenClaw previously had no way to include multiple team members in a single instance without the Claw involved losing its memory. Shared cloud sessions correct that, enabling multiple people to interact with a single Claw while context is maintained across users and a continuous chat, giving OpenClaw feature parity with the agent harnesses offered by frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, which allow collaboration for enterprise users. What about security? Since launching in November 2025, OpenClaw has deservedly earned its reputation as a complete security mess – not only in the code itself but for users and those who are unfortunate enough to come in contact with a Claw’s orders as well. Celebrity UK mathematician Professor Hannah Fry tested OpenClaw out earlier this year, finding it was ready and willing to share her private information when threatened. In another instance, an OpenClaw agent hacked a gym’s waiting list and forced its user into a full class, displacing other reservations, when simply asked to get him on the list. So, what is OpenClaw doing to improve on these risks as part of the update? Not that much, based on a reading of the patch notes. Shared sessions, for example, are a great way to introduce collaborative Claws at work, but the OpenClaw foundation states in the patch notes that the shared session controls “are not tenant isolation or a security boundary.” In other words, you’d better be sure there’s no need to isolate various OpenClaw instances. title: OpenClaw 2.0 pours glitter on slow-burning security dumpster fire

enrich.summary_1line: OpenWALDO, an open-source effort to build a shared AI training dataset, is funded by CIQ and holds 167.3B tokens so far.

text:
Contributors wanted: 167B transparent tokens have a long way to go against AI giants' trillions

A new project aims to build a shared, open source AI training dataset that anyone can contribute to, much like an open source software project. It aims to make training data more transparent than that of many open-weight models that have recently taken the industry by storm. CentOS and Rocky Linux founder Gregory Kurtzer is behind the effort, dubbed Open Weights, Artifacts, Licenses, Data, Origins (OpenWALDO), and it's funded by CIQ, his AI infrastructure company, which also sponsors Rocky Linux. Kurtzer described the effort as trying to bring the open-source ethos to AI model design, which has yet to be truly open – even downloadable open-weight models still have closed-source training data that is unknown to users, alongside other limitations that make them less than truly open source. “I’ve spent my career watching open source turn users into builders, competitors into collaborators, and shared problems into common infrastructure that operates at massive scale,” Kurtzer said in the announcement. “OpenWALDO brings that proven model to AI. Let’s work together, build its foundation in the open, and collaboratively take AI to the next level.” CIQ, which authored the announcement, argues that open-weight models keep that foundation a secret because of where it comes from: Copyrighted data, responses distilled from other models, user-generated content that may not have been given in a truly open manner, and the like. “There is often no way to know what data trained a given model, under what license, or with what consent,” CIQ said, adding that hidden training data content could taint models, putting customer software stacks at risk. In addition to that, there’s the simple fact that, when everyone is training their AI models in secret, a lot of duplicate work is happening that wastes lots of time and computing resources. A single, shared set of public training data, the OpenWALDO team argues, would not only make training more efficient across the industry, but also mean that every improvement to the dataset could benefit future models trained on it. “A lab or company can take the corpus and its bill of materials as a verified baseline, add its own proprietary data, build, and ship, with a clear, auditable line back to its sources,” CIQ explained. With prices steep and ROI still largely absent, open AI models (not to be confused with OpenAI models) have risen to prominence in the AI zeitgeist lately. Models out of the home of open-weight AI, China, are closing in on the capabilities of closed-source frontier lab models like ChatGPT and Claude, leaving many businesses wondering why they ought to pay through the nose for AI services they don’t own, can’t truly control, and have no visibility into. Some frontier labs have warned that open-weight models pose security and misuse risks. Kurtzer argues that open source software faced similar concerns. “Open source has won this argument before,” he said, pointing to similar arguments made about open code, namely that it’s insecure, impossible to trust, and the like. “Linux didn't win by being certified safe. It won by being inspectable, forkable, and community validated.” “AI is missing that same property, and OpenWALDO is how we build it,” Kurtzer said. Turning to open-source training datasets is a big ask for an industry already so far down the closed training data path, of course, and only time will tell if OpenWALDO is a revolution or another obscure OSS project that gets minimal attention from the AI community. So far, the OpenWALDO dataset contains 167.3 billion reference tokens pulled from things like government records, open-source academic papers, mailing lists, and public domain literature - a drop in the bucket next to the tens of trillions of tokens used to train frontier AI models and their open-weight counterparts. enrich.summary_1line: OpenAI launched ChatGPT Business Premium seats at $125/month or $100 annually, offering five times Standard usage.

text:
$125 a month? So, how good are those open-weight models getting, again?

Not getting enough out of that ChatGPT Business subscription? OpenAI is hoping you’ll take it up on a new “premium” Business tier seat that’s up to $100 more a month for some added capacity and higher usage limits. Sam Altman’s AI outfit announced ChatGPT Business Premium seats on Monday, describing the new offering as an option for Business-tier customers who feel they’re chafing under the old Business limitations. Business Premium seats, which can be combined with standard Business seats, get five times more usage than Standard seats, and are exempt from the five-hour-per-day usage limit on advanced features. Those enhanced limits come at a price, though. For reference, standard Business tier seats are $25 a month if paid per month, or $20 per month if billed annually. Premium Business seats, on the other hand, are $125/month or $100 if billed annually. (Larger orgs have their own "call us for pricing" Enterprise tier with all the bells and whistles like SLAs and extra security and access controls.) As for what Premium seats will actually get you, that varies per model and task type. According to a help page for Business models and limits, which doesn’t yet include GPT 5.6 usage limits, GPT 5.5 Instant use is “virtually unlimited” for Business seats. GPT 5.5 Thinking and Pro are limited to 3,000 requests per week and 15 requests per month, respectively. As noted above, Premium seats get 5x that limit. Beyond that, even Premium seats will have to eat into ChatGPT credits, the pay-as-you-go-not-quite-a-token system OpenAI uses to charge for advanced features. OpenAI is running a promotion as part of the launch of Premium Business seats to provide some extra credits for customers who buy into the waitlist for the new offering, with $100 in workspace service credits available for each qualifying Premium seat added to a Business workspace, up to 5 seats. Only the first 10,000 customers to sign up for the Premium waitlist will get those credits, however, so if you’re so inclined, you’d better move fast. Or you could spin up an open-weight model instead Introducing a new, considerably more expensive tokenmaxxing option for smaller business customers at a time when frontier AI labs are being hammered for pushing up prices and facing increased competition from Chinese open-weight models is quite a gamble. Chinese open weights AI models are rapidly becoming just as capable as their closed-source, AI-as-a-service American counterparts, raising the question of why companies with a strategy for heavy AI consumption would be willing to pay hundreds of dollars a month for seat-plus-usage fees when an open-weight model running in a colocation DC or on-prem could deliver similar results. Sure, the hardware isn’t cheap, but the model is free and so is using it, aside from what it costs to keep the server lights blinking. Beyond that, AI returns are still a fuzzy, nebulous thing, too. Plenty of AI investments have yet to pay off; asking customers to pay $100 more a month for increased usage limits is a big ask. Nonetheless, OpenAI is confident that Business Premium seats will be a hot commodity. The new offering, OpenAI claimed to us in an email, was introduced because customers were asking for increased usage limits for deeper work on the Business tier. For them, the company expects the price point to be perfectly acceptable, we’re told. ®
title: Hey, big spender – OpenAI has a new SKU just for you

enrich.summary_1line: UK Department for Business and Trade is consulting on requiring employers to consult workers before deploying workplace monitoring technology.

label.reason: UK workplace surveillance consultation; labor policy, not relevant to his work.

text:
Proposals span AI productivity scores, keystroke logging, biometrics, and other ways to watch workers

The UK government is considering forcing employers in Great Britain to consult workers before rolling out "bossware," opening the door to new rules covering everything from AI-powered productivity scoring to keystroke logging and biometric surveillance. The Department for Business and Trade wants to know whether the rules governing workplace surveillance still make sense as software increasingly tracks employees' activity, measures their performance, and supports decisions that affect their working lives. Ministers haven't settled on an approach. They're asking whether non-statutory guidance would be enough, whether a statutory code of practice is needed, or whether employers should be legally required to consult recognized trade unions or elected employee representatives before introducing workplace monitoring technology (WMT). The consultation says WMT is becoming more common, citing research in which one in three UK organizations said it actively monitored employees' digital activity. Two years earlier, ICO research found the figure stood at one in five employers. The government argues WMT can improve productivity, investment, and economic growth when used well. But it also highlights several pitfalls, warning of "risks to privacy and autonomy," "disproportionate or unnecessary surveillance," and "biased or unfair outcomes" where monitoring systems rely on incomplete or inaccurate data. Artificial intelligence features prominently throughout the consultation, though the proposals extend well beyond AI alone. It notes that WMT can incorporate automated decision-making and algorithmic management, raising questions about transparency, accountability, and the impact of technology on workers. Exactly what counts as workplace monitoring technology, though, is another question. The government is proposing a broad definition covering everything from CCTV and access control systems to biometric technologies, location tracking, keystroke monitoring, productivity software, and systems that incorporate automated decision-making or AI. The consultation asks whether that definition is too broad, too narrow, or about right – an acknowledgment that deciding what qualifies as "bossware" may prove trickier than deciding what to do about it. The consultation, part of the government's broader Make Work Pay reforms, runs until September 30. If ministers impose a statutory consultation duty, compliance teams won't be short of reading material. Stephanie Lees, a data protection specialist at Pinsent Masons, said it would add "a further layer of oversight" for employers already juggling GDPR, local employment laws, and the EU AI Act. It could also mean that rolling out the latest AI-powered workforce optimization suite could become as much an HR exercise as an IT one. ®
title: UK mulls making employers ask before installing bossware

enrich.summary_1line: ShieldFont, an open-source font project, swaps words in raw HTML to mislead LLM scrapers while displaying normal text.

label.reason: Poisoned font against LLM scrapers; mildly interesting novelty, not his core work.

text:
ShieldFont is available today if you've got copy that needs protecting

If you don't want AI scrapers training themselves on your website, there's a new way to stop them that doesn't involve server-side blocking or praying they respect your instructions in robots.txt. A team of creatives have teamed up with a typography company to create a new type of font that’ll trick LLM scrapers into ingesting poisoned gibberish. Dubbed ShieldFont, the open-source project almost seems like magic if you're not familiar with the ins and outs of computer fonts. Look at a web page written using a ShieldFont font and it’ll appear exactly as one would expect: All the content words (the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs that give a sentence meaning) are the same as the writer originally wrote. Inspect the raw HTML that a scraper reads from a ShieldFonted page, however, and you’ll see a sentence that’s essentially gibberish. Typing “good luck reading this, you useless robot” in the online demo version, for example, turns it into “good comfort reading this, you yellow barrier.” The goal, as outlined in the ShieldFont white paper, is not to get a scraping bot to reject the text as garbage, but to convince it that the text on the page is unusual but sensible. A noun will never be swapped for a verb, for example, and a verb will never be swapped for an adjective: Swaps only come from the same grammatical pool. It goes even more distinct than that, The ShieldFont creators noted. “Not just noun for noun: plural abstract noun about communication for plural abstract noun about communication,” the white paper explains. “There are about 250 such pools, built by crossing part of speech with sense category, concreteness, singular or plural, verb transitivity, verb inflection and adjective degree.” Around a quarter of words in a chunk of text end up replaced, the creators noted, with the hope the copy still gets ingested. Even if it doesn't, and the group notes scrapers do sometimes reject it, that still means your writing doesn’t get sucked up to train an AI – a win either way. How does this black magic work? This all seems a bit mystical unless you’re versed in the functions of fonts – specifically fonts in the OpenFont family, which ShieldFont is designed to work with. First off, you may be familiar with typographic ligatures, which combine two letters into a single character for the sake of making text look a bit neater, or conveying meaning in some languages but not others. Æ is one classic example in Latin script used in some languages but not others; there's also ﬁ, which combines a lower case F and I in a way that prevents the top curve of the F from bumping into the I’s dot. OpenType fonts all come with ligature tables that define how single glyphs or glyph sequences get substituted automatically by a word processor in a process known as glyph substitution, or GSUB. Even Google Docs supports user-configurable GSUB to an extent - you can fairly easily configure a substitution to automatically fill in for frequently used special words or characters. ShieldFont works on largely the same premise, but extends GSUB to entire words instead of letters or character pairs. So for example, a word like "daughter" in raw HTML might be rendered as "journalist" when it actually shows up to human viewers on the page. Here's what a paragraph written in the ShieldFont looks like as viewed on a web page (above), as opposed to what the raw HTML actually says (below): Even with that extended GSUB format, the font files are still quite small. We spoke with Amsterdam design studio Seneda & Abrucio, founded by Isaque Seneda and Gabriel Abrucio, the team behind ShieldFont, and they told us that the document/desktop fonts that are ShieldFonted are only around 5 MB, while compressed web fonts that include the entire GSUB dictionary still only come in at around 800 KB - large for your average font, S&A explained, but still considerably smaller than the desktop version.
