enrich.summary_1line: Autopilot-Jobhunt, a Python project by Tarun Gupta, scans the web for jobs, scores matches against a resume and sends results via Telegram.

label.reason: Python AI job-hunt agent project; loosely related hobby tool, thin.

text:
Searching for work sucks; AI combs the internet and sucks it all up. Combine the two and let 'er rip with this Python project

Combing through job postings and company help wanted pages for a position that matches your resume is the very definition of drudge work. Now, there's an AI designed to suck up information from the web, do the search for you, and even help you apply. Software developer Tarun Gupta created just such a tool in the form of Autopilot-Jobhunt. When configured with a profile of the user and their desired jobs (and what they absolutely won’t accept in an opening), A-J will scan the web while users sleep, take stock of the positions that are a good match, and then send a Telegram message to its user. That message includes all matching openings, scored against the user's resume and ranked according to the AI's assessment. Users can ask A-J to format a resume and cover letter tailored to the position, which it’s up to the user to review and send - the bot won’t do so automatically. You might be thinking that an AI-crafted resume and cover letter would be a bad strategy for getting your foot in the door at a company you’re keen to work for, but that might not be the case, actually. As we reported last year, researchers found that some AI hiring bots, often the first line a company uses to separate the wheat from the chaff, favored applications generated by the same AI model they used for screening - suggesting the human touch may be worth less than you think in the modern job market. A-J is designed to be free to use (what hard-up developer can afford to do hundreds of AI API calls a night, after all?), and relies on free models to comb the web for jobs. TinyFish’s AI web agent is used to crawl for jobs, while OpenRouter provides the API for one of several default free AI models that A-J will run through, starting with Llama and falling back to free versions of Nvidia’s Nemotron, Google’s Gemma 4, and Alibaba’s Qwen3 when all else fails, or quotas run out. Claude Code and the Anthropic API can be used in place of OpenRouter if you’ve got tokens to spare. For those concerned about A-J broadcasting personal details to the web, Gupta writes that it’s designed to be private, providing an entire privacy readme as part of the project’s GitHub documentation. As mentioned above, A-J never applies for a job on a user’s behalf, and the config file where users link to their locally stored Markdown-formatted resume and set other options is gitignored so it won’t ever be committed by accident. That said, resumes do get routed to the LLMs OpenRouter is configured to use. Gupta said those who want to avoid sending that data through OpenRouter can use Claude Code instead, provided they have an Anthropic subscription that supports it. As for who could make use of the tool, it’s configured by default for software developers, and for good reason: According to Hiring Lab data published on Wednesday, the number of job openings for software developers has risen by 15 percent since Anthropic released Claude Code in February 2025, while openings for all other jobs have fallen by seven percent over the same timeframe. Still, young college graduates in a variety of career fields report not being able to find a job, so the tool could be of use to anyone with the willingness to reconfigure it for a different career field. AI companies, fintechs, and Silicon Valley heavyweights might be programmed into A-J by default, but they can be freely added, removed, and reconfigured as desired. It’ll probably take some work to get Autopilot-Jobhunt configured for your particular needs, but if you’re having trouble landing a role, giving it a shot can’t hurt. ®
title: AI tool scours the web for job openings, preps your resume and cover letter

enrich.summary_1line: OpenAI president Greg Brockman testified in court that the company expects to spend $50 billion on computing this year.

label.reason: OpenAI's $50B compute burn from court testimony; business context, no engineering impact.

text:
If the numbers are large enough, perhaps we won't question the math

An executive for ChatGPT maker OpenAI said in court testimony on Tuesday that the AI model developer expects to burn $50 billion on computing power before the end of the year. Cofounder and president Greg Brockman threw out the number, which was previously reported by Bloomberg, during OpenAI's closely watched legal battle with hype-fiend Elon Musk. If it wasn't obvious, that would be $50 billion of someone else's money. Nearly four years after ChatGPT kicked off the AI boom, OpenAI's leadership hasn't yet figured out how to turn a profit. Heck, the company can't even manage to hit its own revenue targets, if recent reports are to be believed. That hasn't stopped CEO Sam Altman from talking the likes of Microsoft, Amazon, SoftBank, Nvidia and others into issuing press releases claiming plans to invest tens of billions of dollars into his quest for AGI. (Or was it AI superintelligence? The goalposts haven't exactly been fixed in concrete.) We're not sure if "investment" adequately captures the roundabout financial engineering that's gone into these highly publicized deals. Many are contingent on OpenAI using some of the pledged cash to lease massive quantities of compute either directly from its backers or their partners. Back in February, Amazon, Nvidia, and SoftBank announced a $110 billion investment in the AI startup, at least $80 billion of which came with strings attached. For example, OpenAI would need to rent two gigawatts of Amazon's Trainium AI accelerators and deploy its top GPT models in AWS to claim $35 billion of the $50 billion promised by the cloud titan. Similarly, Nvidia's $30 billion investment was tied to the deployment of five gigawatts of training and inference compute capacity at an estimated cost of $300 billion. In other words, these companies' investments in OpenAI are really more of a discount or rebate. It raises the question: Can OpenAI actually burn $50 billion in 2026, or is it simply throwing out more big numbers in hopes of maintaining an air of unassailable momentum? Place your bets – ideally in the form of burning as many heavily subsidized tokens as you can now, before prices inevitably rise. We've reached out to OpenAI for comment; we'll let you know if we hear anything back. ®
title: OpenAI exec says company hopes to burn $50B of somebody else's money on compute this year

enrich.summary_1line: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter MoE with 17B active parameters; weights are closed at launch.

label.reason: New 594B MoE model, 17B active, Apache 2.0 weights planned; significant open-weights LLM release.

text:
Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter MoE with 17B active parameters. It scores 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and runs on Tinker, with Apache 2.0 weights planned. Together AI has introduced Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven system that keeps re-optimizing inference as production traffic changes. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop. TL;DR System: It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B. Runs on: NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X and AWS Trainium2. Each run used at most 2 nodes per model. Performance: Up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best published InferenceX configurations, in under 24 hours per setting. Best: 1,111 P90 TPS per user on MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200, batch size 1), 1.8x over the 633 TPS baseline. Worst: GLM 5.3 on MI355X moved only from 463 to 480 TPS (about 4%). What is Together Compiler? Together Compiler is a continual compilation loop from Together AI that uses coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass. It takes a server launch command, a traffic profile and a hardware configuration. Agents propose faster forward passes, and a persistent engine measures each one. The winning code ships into the serving engine. When traffic drifts, the loop runs again. Why does inference need continual compilation? Together AI team reports that its traffic shape never sits still. Prompt lengths in one country ran about 97K tokens versus 70K elsewhere. One customer’s P90 input length grew from 18K to 33K tokens in 3 days. Kernels tuned on random data can also mislead. Random inputs activated 13 to 38% more MoE experts than real traffic. One agent-written top-k kernel took 20 µs on random data. On real data at 70K context, it took up to 62 ms. How does the persistent engine work? Most agent loops restart vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM for every experiment. The research team measures 761 seconds of cold startup for MiniMax M3.1 Flash on TensorRT-LLM. Together Compiler starts the engine once. Agents submit a candidate forward pass over RPC. The server swaps the forward function pointer and re-captures CUDA graphs. Two measurement tiers balance speed and fidelity. A fast tier serves 12 layers for quick screening. A slow tier serves 60 layers to confirm gains on real distributions. Two tiers tested 8.1x more candidates than one slow tier (1,354 vs 168). They also found a solution 7.2% faster. Together AI team reports 252x higher agent experiment throughput than an engine-restart baseline. How does it choose a parallelism layout? A cost model ranks tensor, expert, data and context parallel layouts before agents start. It mixes spec-sheet numbers, microbenchmarks and measured forward passes. It also uses measured MoE expert imbalance and uneven request lengths. On Kimi K3, it found a production layout with up to 24% higher TPS. What did agents need from human experts? An expert-curated knowledge base produced 25 to 31% lower speedup after 12 hours. Naive agents told to make the forward pass “as fast as possible” beat expert strategies. The ensemble scores were 6.2x versus 4.9x after 10 trials. Custom logging structures ate up to 43% of tool calls. Google Research has released Agile Deliberation, a human-in-the-loop framework for building image classifiers around subjective concepts. Think ‘healthy food’, ‘inspiring artwork’ or clickbait in content moderation. Most tooling assumes users already know the concept boundary. Agile Deliberation assumes they do not, and helps them find it. Agile Deliberation is a Google Research’s framework that turns a vague concept into a structured written definition. That definition does two jobs. It is a human-readable policy, and it is the text prompt for a VLM classifier. Each round keeps the candidate definition with the best F1 on the user’s labels. The design came from interviews with a group of content moderation experts. Experts scoped a concept first, then refined it on borderline images. Finding those images was the slow part. Stage 1 breaks the concept into at most 3 unit concepts, using prompt chaining with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Each unit gets candidate positive and negative subconcepts, shown with retrieved images. For healthy food, positives might be salads or grain bowls. Negatives might be processed food or raw, unprepared ingredients. The user keeps, flips or drops each one. Stage 2 skips classic uncertainty sampling. The classifier is a prompted generative VLM, so its confidence scores are often uncalibrated. Instead, the system hunts for images that are borderline in meaning. The pipeline runs 4 steps: Users label each image and add short notes on disagreements. An LLM turns those notes into candidate definitions. A greedy update keeps the best-scoring one. Subjective concepts have no fixed ground truth, so Google team skipped static benchmarks. It ran 18 live sessions of about 90 minutes each. 9 participants without professional moderation experience did 2 sessions each. One session used Agile Deliberation, the other used manual deliberation. Each participant spent about 45 minutes defining a concept, then labeled 200 held-out test images. The two concepts were ‘paid to play’ clickbait and ‘healthy food’. Retrieval ran over a proprietary 100M-image dataset and WebLI, respectively. Source: Table 1 of the CVPR 2026 paper. F1 averaged over participants. The repo ships a Demo.ipynb that walks through the healthy food example. It needs a Gemini API key and defaults to gemini-2.5-pro and gemini-2.5-flash. enrich.summary_1line: Delhi High Court rejected Unity Small Finance Bank's appeal against an interim order barring a capital restructuring resolution without prior consent from RIPL and Centrum.

text: Adding another layer to the ongoing shareholder dispute at BharatPe-backed Unity Small Finance Bank (SFB), the Delhi High Court (HC) has rejected an appeal filed by the bank against an interim order. The interim order restrains Unity SFB from placing a proposed capital restructuring resolution before its board without prior written consent from BharatPe parent Resilient Innovations (RIPL) and Centrum Financial Services. The order, passed by a bench Justices C Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar on November 5, restrains Unity SFB from tabling, discussing or approving ‘Agenda Item 18’ at its board meeting without prior written consent from RIPL and Centrum Financial Services. The HC granted BharatPe the interim relief pertaining to the case earlier this year in July The dispute stems from a Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) signed between Unity Bank, RIPL and Centrum in October 2021, following their partnership to establish Unity SFB. The agreement features certain ‘Reserved Matters’ that would require prior written consent from representatives of both RIPL and Centrum. These include changes to the bank’s capital structure and amendments to its constitutional documents. Agenda Item 18 proposed increasing Unity SFB’s authorised share capital from ₹4,000 Cr to ₹4,900 Cr by creating an additional 90 Cr preference shares of ₹10 each. The proposal also involved amending the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MoA) to facilitate the issuance of these shares. RIPL opposed the proposal, arguing that the proposed capital restructuring could dilute its shareholding in Unity SFB from 49% to 21%. It contended that the resolution fell under the SHA’s Reserved Matters and therefore required prior written consent from both RIPL and Centrum. Welcoming the decision, BharatPe said the ruling reaffirmed the shareholder rights and governance framework agreed upon when the joint venture was established in 2021. “The board must ensure that the bank complies with the court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders,” a BharatPe spokesperson said. The company also called on Unity’s board to respect the governance processes agreed upon at the time of the bank’s inception and honour its contractual obligations under the SHA. It said the agreed framework should not be set aside to favour one shareholder group over another. Unity Small Bank, on the other hand, declined to comment on the matter. “The discussions are solely between the bank’s promoter and a financial investor. The bank remains operationally unaffected, and continues to serve its customers and stakeholders as usual,” the bank told Inc42. The proposal also involved amending Clause V of the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MOA) to reflect the revised authorised capital. enrich.summary_1line: X told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices attributed to Delhi Police against IFF and SFLC.in were fake.

text: Social media platform X has told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices purportedly issued by the Delhi Police against digital rights organisations Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC.in) were fake. According to a post by IFF today, X said an internal investigation found the purported police communications to be fake and that it had filed a complaint with law enforcement authorities. X’s counsel told the court that an imposter had submitted the requests in the Delhi Police’s name. “X stated that it is not likely to take any action at this stage,” IFF’s post added. The court recorded X’s statement and disposed of the organisations’ petitions, granting them liberty to approach it again if the platform takes action against their accounts. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, representing both organisations, placed X’s transparency reports and a legal notice purportedly sent on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) on record. IFF said it had written to the RSS seeking confirmation of the legal notice’s authenticity but received no response. Separately, SFLC.in said an email seeking verification of the takedown requests had bounced back from the Delhi Police address mentioned in the communication. IFF said X forwarded two ‘Illegal Content Reports’ to it on Tuesday (November 3), submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police. The first, dated October 31, sought the removal of a post IFF published on October 30 and another by SFLC.in. The second, dated Monday (November 2), sought the removal of 37 posts and the withholding of the accounts of IFF, SFLC.in, and GeoBlockedIndia. The reports alleged that the posts defamed the RSS under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The posts reproduced and commented on a legal notice the organisations said they had received in the RSS’s name. IFF contested the requests, arguing that its posts were protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. It also questioned their legal basis, saying the reports cited no complaint, FIR, Magistrate’s order, or court order. Through its counsel, IFF subsequently served a legal notice to the Delhi Police, with a copy to X, seeking withdrawal of the reports and details of the authority under which they had been submitted. It also asked X not to act on the requests pending their withdrawal or adjudication. IFF approached the Delhi High Court after receiving no official withdrawal or clarification from the Delhi Police. The dispute comes amid a wider debate over content takedowns, transparency, and platforms’ responsibilities when responding to government requests. In July, former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey claimed that the Indian government had directed GitHub to remove three URLs linked to bitchat, an open-source messaging app that enables peer-to-peer communication without internet connectivity or centralised servers. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre’s (I4C) reported directive gave GitHub three hours to remove or disable access to the URLs. These covered the project’s main source code repository, Android repository, and Android releases page. The agency cited concerns over anonymous communication and difficulties in lawful interception and investigations. Meanwhile, MeitY is reportedly exploring withdrawing safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000, from social media platforms. The provision limits intermediaries’ liability for third-party content, subject to prescribed conditions. enrich.summary_1line: TRAI recommended a separate satellite network provider authorisation and proposed direct-to-device satellite services, subject to government approval.

label.reason: TRAI satellite direct-to-device telecom policy; unrelated to AI engineering.

text: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum. The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage. Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation. The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services. The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships. For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation. In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage. However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation. The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years. TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators. For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India. For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity. However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use. TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them. TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee. Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator. Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz. For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue. The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market. text: Fintech soonicorn Cashfree Payments has launched ‘Checkout for Agents’, a new tool that enables AI agents to process customer payments seamlessly. The new feature is built on the open-source WebMCP (model context protocol). The startup claims that merchants using Cashfree’s checkout page can avail the service without requiring any code changes or technical updates. The new solution aims to address a critical friction point in agentic commerce. While global purchases initiated by AI agents are projected to hit $1.5 Tn by 2030, traditional web interfaces remain optimised for human navigation. Hence, AI agents consume nearly 2 Mn tokens on average to decode the web page when they need to execute a transaction. By leveraging WebMCP, Cashfree claims that its new checkout tool directly communicates all the available actions to the AI agents, including reading order total and selecting payment mode. The startup claims its solution reduces token consumption by over 40%. The architecture also allows personal AI assistants like Instinct, Meta’s Muse, and Grok Bot to reach the final payment step with fewer errors and lower drop-off rates, while leaving the final transaction authorisation with the user. “If an agent is visiting and browsing the merchant’s website, there will not be any drop off at the payment layer. Your speed of conversion will increase, token usage will drop, and the success rate will be near 100% as far as an agent making a payment is concerned,” Cashfree cofounder Reeju Datta told Inc42. He foresees AI agents driving a significant share of traffic to Cashfree’s customers in the future. “Agent traffic has grown around 4-5X annually and converts 5X better than my SEO traffic. The lifetime value (LTV) of such users is also much much higher,” Datta added. On a question about AI agents taking unauthorised or unintended actions, Datta claimed that Cashfree’s latest offering preserves existing authorisation mechanisms and creates no heightened vulnerabilities. For instance, if the final payment authorisation step requires an OTP, then the user would still have to enter the pin to approve the payment. Founded in 2015 by Datta and Akash Sinha, Cashfree Payments offers digital payment solutions such as payment gateway, cross-border payments, payout solutions and banking APIs. It claims to process over $80 Bn in annual transaction volumes for over 10 Lakh businesses, including the likes of MakeMyTrip, Zomato, CRED, and Delhivery. Cashfree isn’t the only one in India’s startup ecosystem betting on agentic commerce. Its IPO-bound rival Razorpay is also repositioning itself as an AI-powered business operating system through its Agent Studio and agentic commerce push. Then, there is Bengaluru-based Nudge that helps ecommerce brands optimise product discovery and conversions inside AI platforms. Foodtech giant Swiggy is also enabling users to interact with its app through external AI agents to discover food, build carts, place orders, and book restaurant tables. The mission was designed to test the startup’s soft robotic capture system that removes space debris, but the system’s robotic petals failed to deploy as intended. The startup is now gearing up for Embrace-2, an upgraded version of the mission to validate its upgraded robotic capture mechanism, which is expected to launch in the coming months. This includes simulating how objects behave in microgravity (near-weightlessness) and how they appear or function under space-like visual conditions. This costs around ₹6 Cr to construct, per Phanindra. Base 1 houses infrastructure for designing, building and testing satellite servicing and space debris recovery missions. enrich.summary_1line: CERT-In issued a November 4, 2026 advisory on an AI-assisted campaign, CRAFTY FALCON, targeting payment and disbursement APIs at BFSI entities.

label.reason: CERT-In advisory on AI-driven attacks exploiting payment APIs; useful security awareness for API builders.

text: India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has issued a critical warning to entities in the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector over an escalating campaign of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting payment and disbursement APIs. In an advisory dated November 4, 2026, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) identified the threat actor behind the campaign as ‘CRAFTY FALCON’, describing it as an AI-assisted financial threat actor that uses machine intelligence to identify targets, execute attacks at machine speed and exploit victims’ own payment and disbursement APIs to initiate unauthorised fund transfers. Banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), fintech companies and other financial services entities have been warned of the growing threat. CERT-In’s Computer Security Incident Response Team-Finance (CSIRT-Fin) said the campaign has witnessed a significant escalation, with successful attacks continuing to be reported across the financial services ecosystem. The agency has urged all BFSI entities to treat the campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. A key concern highlighted in the advisory is the threat actor’s continued targeting of financial entities that had already received earlier restricted advisories and undertaken remediation measures. According to CERT-In, some of these organisations have been deliberately targeted again, including cases where remediation was incomplete. The attacks have also been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other periods of reduced monitoring, potentially delaying detection and response. CERT-In’s analysis identified the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools in the campaign. These include the ARTEX family of large language model (LLM)-based tools, PentAGI, an autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system, and the Cairn attack search engine, alongside the CyberStrikeAI framework. These tools can execute complete attack chains autonomously, generate and refine large volumes of customised attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on responses from targeted systems. The supporting attack infrastructure also changes frequently, with IP addresses rotating within hours to days. CERT-In said infrastructure fingerprints and detailed detection rules have been shared with affected entities through restricted advisories. The latest advisory follows another critical warning issued by CERT-In in October, when the agency flagged attackers using publicly available agentic AI tools to conduct financially motivated intrusions into Indian organisations. The watchdog warned that autonomous AI agents, ostensibly deployed for research and evaluation, had accessed live systems without authorisation, reading business records containing personal data and confidential information. Meanwhile, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has also warned banks, NBFCs and fintech startups about the growing use of AI agents by cybercriminals to perpetrate financial fraud. The agency said it had uncovered multiple individual cases in which malicious agentic AI systems exploited compromised financial systems to execute unauthorised transactions involving amounts running into crores of rupees. Separately, CERT-In has flagged multiple vulnerabilities in select versions of Tata Motors’ iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev connected vehicle applications, which could allow attackers to access sensitive credentials and vehicle-related information. The agency identified four vulnerabilities, including hardcoded service account credentials, API keys and authorisation tokens within the applications; inadequate validation of URLs and origins loaded through the apps’ WebView component; authentication tokens being recorded in application logs; and improper implementation of SSL certificate pinning in the network security configuration. enrich.summary_1line: Shiprocket reported a consolidated net profit of ₹0.6 Cr for Q2 FY27, against a ₹20.3 Cr loss a year earlier, on 34.7% revenue growth.

text: Ecommerce enablement platform Shiprocket turned profitable in the September quarter, reporting a consolidated net profit of ₹0.6 Cr against a net loss of ₹20.3 Cr in Q2 FY26. Operating revenue rose 34.7% to ₹673.6 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹500.2 Cr a year ago. Shiprocket, which listed on the NSE and BSE in August, had posted a net loss of ₹13.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. Sequentially, operating revenue increased 13.8% from ₹592.1 Cr. Revenue grew faster than expenditure during the quarter, with total expenses increasing 29.6% to ₹692.9 Cr from ₹534.8 Cr. Other income increased to ₹19.9 Cr from ₹14.3 Cr, taking total income to ₹693.5 Cr, marginally above total expenses. The company reported no tax expense for the quarter. Shiprocket’s adjusted EBITDA rose to ₹14.2 Cr from ₹4.3 Cr a year ago, while its adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 2.1% from 0.9%. Shiprocket reports its operations under two segments: core business and emerging business. The latter includes marketing technology, checkout, cross-border, and omnichannel solutions. Core business revenue grew 25.3% to ₹461.5 Cr from ₹368.3 Cr a year ago, while adjusted EBITDA increased 28.9% to ₹59.1 Cr. The segment’s adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 12.8% from 12.4%, with transactions growing 31% during the quarter. Emerging business revenue rose 60.9% to ₹212.2 Cr from ₹131.9 Cr, increasing its share of overall revenue to 31% from 26%. However, the segment’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹44.9 Cr from ₹41.6 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA loss margin narrowed to 21.2% from 31.5%, reflecting faster revenue growth. Within emerging businesses, martech revenue jumped 102%, while omnichannel revenue rose 79%. Shiprocket attributed omnichannel growth to brands using its services to replenish quick commerce dark stores, including appointment-based deliveries with visibility into purchase orders from platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto. Its martech offerings, grouped under Fastrr, span advertising, checkout, and customer engagement tools. Shiprocket processed 233 Mn unique transactions involving goods worth ₹37,398.7 Cr in gross merchandise value (GMV) during the trailing 12 months ended September 30. It served 2.36 Lakh active merchants over the same period. For Q2 FY27, the company reported 33% growth in GMV, 34% growth in transactions, an 8% increase in merchants, and a 25% rise in average revenue per user. The number of merchants using its emerging business offerings increased 75% to 62,025 on a trailing 12-month basis. Meanwhile, 9.3% of core business merchants used an emerging product, up from 7.9% a year ago. Around 17,300 new merchants joined Shiprocket through its emerging products during the quarter, compared with about 5,400 a year earlier. CFO Tanmay Kumar attributed the turnaround to growth in core business transactions, improving contribution from emerging businesses, and the repayment of borrowings using IPO proceeds. “… IPO proceeds retired all our borrowings, which cut finance costs, and the surplus now earns interest income,” Kumar said. Finance costs declined to ₹4.9 Cr from ₹6.7 Cr a year ago. The company had no outstanding borrowings at September-end as against ₹242 Cr at March 31, although lease liabilities remained on its books. Net cash generated from operating activities stood at ₹55.1 Cr in H1 FY27 compared with ₹23.8 Cr a year ago. Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Gautam Kapoor, Vishesh Khurana, and Akshay Ghulati, Shiprocket started as a logistics aggregator for online sellers, partnering with third-party delivery providers. It has since expanded into a broader ecommerce enablement platform. Important to highlight that Khurana left operational role at Shiprocket in 2025 to join Tribe Capital, Shiprocket’s backer, as a managing partner. enrich.summary_1line: Deepinder Goyal defended the Temple brain-monitoring wearable on X after criticism from Indian doctors who questioned its scientific evidence.

text:
In a post on X, Goyal said $30 million was invested in building the device, of which he put in $20 million of his personal money.

Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building. “The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. Criticising the doctors, he said, "All my emotion last night was directed at a few influencer doctors, who are more influencers than doctors. They did not read our research in detail, and spread twisted facts to call something new a scam. They get views by piling on us." The open debate started on Thursday when Goyal took to X to defend the device. He said, “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple.” He also said the device features a 14-day no-question return policy. “If the product doesn't work, it fails out of the gate and the company dies before recovering a tenth of its R&D," he said. Goyal is currently Vice Chairman and Non-Executive Director of Eternal (parent company of Zomato). He is also the founder of healthtech wearable startup Temple and LAT Aerospace. In the post, Goyal highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money. Calling this his purpose, he said it's not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.” Goyal argued that most wearable companies start with internal studies. He referred to Whoop which shipped its fitness band in 2015 but the first published validation happened a few years later. He also added that Temple had a higher standard. "Pre-prints are a step prior to peer reviewed publications, and they are coming up." Reposing confidence in the product, he said, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.” Moreover, he added that this device is a fitness tracker, and wellness device, not a medical device. “If at some point, we clinically validate any of our metrics, we will let you know.” However, some doctors were not convinced by Goyal’s response. Responding to Goyal's claim on showing scientific evidence, an X user, who goes by the handle TheLiverdoc, said the Apple Watch Series 11 and Fitbit Sense had shown clinical evidence before launch. Similarly, Samsung Galaxy Watch8 and Watch9 also passed FDA trials prior to release. "Meanwhile, the Oura Ring 4 and Whoop 4.0 launched as wellness trackers backed by peer-reviewed sleep studies." On X, Dr Rishabh Jain responded saying Goyal shared financial and personal sacrifices but no scientific evidence. "Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny 'rage'. You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return policies, personal reputation, and promises of future studies. None of these constitutes scientific validation.” Criticising the return policy he said, "Subjective satisfaction cannot establish medical accuracy.” Dr Jain further said that doctors are not against innovation. However the evidence needs to show it. "If Temple delivers what it promises, doctors will be among its biggest supporters." He also said that science is not a popularity contest, and criticism is not “rage". Dr Jain also asked for data that can be reviewed by independent researchers. Temple is a wearable device that tracks blood flow and oxyge
title: Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple

enrich.summary_1line: VeloDB's APAC director argued at TechSparks 2026 that AI agents need a unified real-time data layer to move from pilot to production.

label.reason: Why agents fail in production, data layer/database angle; relevant, though vendor keynote.

text:
At TechSparks 2026, VeloDB’s Regional Director for APAC explained why AI agents that work in pilots struggle in production, and why the fix often lies in the database underneath them.

AI agents tend to look good in a pilot. The scope is narrow, the data is controlled, and the questions are predictable. Production is different, and that gap is where many projects stall. Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. For Nitin Waghulde, Regional Director, APAC at VeloDB, a large part of the problem sits below the model, in the data layer. In a keynote titled ‘AI agents at scale: Surviving beyond the demo’, Nitin explained how AI agents use data differently from people, what they need to work reliably at scale, and how companies are redesigning their data infrastructure to support them. Nitin started his session with an example. In a traditional system, a business manager who wanted last year’s sales figure would run a ready-made report and get the number in one lookup. Ask an AI agent why sales dropped over the last three quarters, and the work changes. The agent pulls order records from the ERP and CRM systems, scans support tickets and chats to check whether major customers have escalated problems, and reads sales team reports on territory dynamics. If its reasoning is incomplete, it goes back for more. “What used to be completed in one simple lookup or one simple query, now you’re taking hundreds of lookups for the same thing,” he said. In the past, people and reports were the main consumers of business data, and systems were built around fixed reports with clear boundaries. Now, Nitin said, AI has become a new customer of that data, and it behaves very differently. Agents run around the clock, ask many questions at once, and work in an iterative loop: ask, think, search, and retry until they can answer. Their questions are also unscripted. That puts a heavy, unpredictable load on the data layer. The challenge grows because business data lives in several places at once: transactional records, chat memory, documents, dashboards and pre-built reports, and vector stores for meaning-based search. An agent has to search all of them and combine the results before it can answer. Each extra trip to the data adds cost. If the data is stale, the answer is wrong. Nitin compared it to driving with an inaccurate traffic map. And when data comes from many sources, it becomes harder to know where an answer came from, which creates a trust problem. He likened it to sending someone to five filing cabinets to collect pieces of paper. By the time the person returns from the fifth cabinet, the information from the first may already be out of date. Nitin outlined four requirements for agents to move from pilot to production. VeloDB’s answer is a single engine that handles all of these needs. The company was founded in 2023 by the original creators of Apache Doris, an open-source real-time analytics database that became a top-level Apache Software Foundation project in June 2022. According to VeloDB, Apache Doris has more than 14,000 GitHub stars and 700 contributors, and is used by over 5,000 enterprises worldwide. To cut down the back-and-forth trips that slow agents down, VeloDB supports hybrid queries. A single query can combine SQL, vector search, and text search, running deterministic and probabilistic searches in parallel. The result is one unified source of truth instead of scattered data. Nitin shared two examples of companies running this architecture in production. The first was one of the largest crypto exchanges, with more than 120 million users, which he did not name. The exchange makes transaction data available to AI agents that retail investors can query, for example to see what positions large traders are taking on an asset. He said its agents handle about 33,000 conversations with a tail latency of around 3

enrich.summary_1line: Delhi High Court division bench dismissed Unity Bank's appeal, upholding BharatPe parent RIPL's shareholder consent rights under the SHA.

text: A division bench of the Delhi High Court has dismissed an appeal by Unity Bank, upholding the interim protection granted to BharatPe's parent company RIPL (Resilient Innovations Private Limited) under the Shareholders’ Agreement and affirming the order of a single judge. The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires. Rejecting the bank’s explanation that it had sought RIPL’s consent on Reserved Matters through an “inadvertent error”, the bench called the plea an “argument of desperation and nothing more”. It noted that Unity had expressly sought RIPL’s consent in writing, which showed it knew of the contractual requirement. The bench reaffirmed that Unity cannot take decisions on Reserved Matters without the prior written consent of RIPL and Centrum, observing that Clause 8 of the SHA explicitly bars any action on such matters without it. It endorsed the single judge’s findings, describing the matter as “elementary”. The court also rejected Unity’s contention that the Reserve Bank of India had turned down the SHA. It observed that the RBI had never objected to the agreement, which had been submitted to it for approval, and held that the injunction does not obstruct any RBI directive and merely requires enforcement of Clause 8. Turning down the argument that the SHA cannot override the Articles of Association, the bench noted that Clause 8 opens with a non obstante clause, giving it precedence over the relevant provisions of the Articles. BharatPe welcomed the decision. A spokesperson said, “The Board must ensure that the Bank complies with the Court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the Board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the Bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders. Governance processes followed since the Bank’s inception must be respected and applied consistently. They cannot be set aside to favour one shareholder group at the expense of another. “We expect the Board to guide the Bank in honouring its contractual obligations and ensuring that its actions comply with the Court’s directions. We believe the Hon’ble Division Bench’s decision reinforces the importance of the agreed governance framework and the shareholder rights that formed the basis of the joint venture in 2021. Respect for these commitments is essential to maintaining trust between shareholders and protecting the institution’s long-term interests.” The ruling reinforces that Unity Bank is bound by the Reserved Matter provisions of the SHA and cannot dismiss its own written requests for shareholder consent as inadvertent errors to avoid its contractual obligations.
title: Delhi HC upholds interim protection for BharatPe’s shareholder rights, dismisses Unity Bank’s appeal

text:
How did Bihar Museum enter the global top 10? Shradha Sharma reflects on Nitish Kumar's vision, legal challenges and the persistence behind its success

Bihar Museum in Patna was recently ranked ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris. The museum has secured the ninth place on The World's 100 Best Museums 2026, published by German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met stands tenth and the Louvre 31st. It is the only Indian institution on the list and the highest-ranked museum in Asia. For a museum that opened barely a decade ago, it is a significant achievement. More so because there was a time when the project itself faced serious opposition, with questions raised about its cost, relevance and the way it was being executed. Reflecting on the recognition in a recent LinkedIn post, YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma recalled the roles played by two people in getting the museum built: Nitish Kumar, who championed the project as Bihar's Chief Minister, and 1992-batch IAS officer Chanchal Kumar, who was entrusted with its execution. When the state government proposed spending nearly Rs 500 crore on a world-class museum in Patna, the decision attracted criticism. Why should a state struggling with basic infrastructure invest so much in a museum? Who would visit it? Could the money have been better spent elsewhere? According to Sharma, even people within the political establishment questioned the proposal. Nitish Kumar, however, stood by the project, convinced that Bihar needed an institution worthy of its historical and cultural heritage. The challenges began with the land. According to Sharma, the proposed 13-acre site had seven government bungalows, some occupied by senior officials and a state minister. Getting the occupants to vacate required considerable administrative effort and legal intervention. She also recounted an incident in which men allegedly linked to local politicians entered the construction site demanding subcontracts, prompting police intervention. The museum was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki in collaboration with Mumbai-based architectural firm Opolis, while Larsen & Toubro was selected to construct it. But appointing internationally recognised architects and an established construction company was only part of the challenge. Getting the project completed was another matter. The museum also faced judicial scrutiny. In June 2015, the Patna High Court, hearing a public interest litigation, criticised the expenditure of approximately Rs 500 crore and questioned the transparency of the contracting process. The court held that the project was not in the public interest but declined to halt construction because the building was nearing completion. Those findings remain an important part of the museum's history. Its international recognition does not erase the questions raised about public spending and governance, although the institution has since gained recognition well beyond Bihar. Sharma credits much of the execution to Chanchal Kumar, who held the dual responsibility of Secretary of Art and Culture and Secretary of the Building Construction Department. The arrangement meant that both the museum's cultural vision and its construction came under the same officer. Sharma said she recently read his account of how the museum came together and was struck by how little he spoke about his own contribution. Behind the finished building were years of navigating approvals, land disputes, administrative resistance and the many complications that accompany a large public project. In Sharma's telling, Nitish Kumar's political backing and Chanchal Kumar's persistence were crucial to seeing it through. For Sharma, who grew up in Bihar, the recognition carries a more personal meaning. Few places in India can claim the kind of historical and intellectual inheritance that Bihar possesses. enrich.summary_1line: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora argues vulnerability patching lags AI-driven discovery and recommends virtual patching and shared clearing houses.

entities: company:national institute of standards and technology
text:
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, has called for faster and more collaborative approaches to vulnerability management.

Nikesh Arora, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Palo Alto Networks, has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify software vulnerabilities and link them into potential attack paths. While these capabilities can help strengthen cybersecurity, they could also give attackers faster ways to exploit weaknesses in enterprise systems. The bigger challenge, Arora notes in a LinkedIn post, is ensuring that organisations can verify, prioritise and fix vulnerabilities at the same pace at which AI can discover them. “Most organizations do not have capacity to patch at the speed needed, especially the smaller ones,” Arora wrote. Smaller businesses often lack security specialists, while larger ones must test fixes against existing applications. He also says models identify different weaknesses, so one model cannot provide complete coverage. Finding a flaw is only the start. Teams must confirm it, assess the risk, develop a fix, test for disruption and deploy it. False positives, or incorrect alerts, waste time, while untested patches can disrupt services. The scale is growing. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology said submissions to its National Vulnerability Database rose 263% between 2020 and 2025. It enriched nearly 42,000 records in 2025, but this was still insufficient. In April 2026, it adopted risk-based prioritisation, focusing on exploited flaws and critical software. AI developers are linking discovery with repair. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, launched in April 2026 with Palo Alto Networks among its partners, gives selected organisations access to Claude Mythos Preview for defensive security. Anthropic said partners had identified more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaws by June and expanded the programme to around 150 additional organisations. On November 4, OpenAI reported that a controlled Linux-kernel pipeline generated candidate patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, which allow a user to gain higher access rights. Human researchers reviewed the findings before reporting them to maintainers. In India, CERT-In’s November 4 advisory warned of an AI-assisted threat actor targeting non-bank lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and cryptocurrency platforms through machine intelligence and payment APIs. The agency has also issued 2026 guidance on AI-assisted vulnerability defence and AI security auditing. Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure. “The most obvious solution is virtual patching. This is a time tested technology that is currently available with cyber vendors for endpoints, WAF, cloud, network use cases.” WAF is a web application firewall, which filters website and application traffic. A virtual patch is a security rule that blocks a known method of exploiting a flaw without changing the affected software. It buys time while a permanent update is tested, but does not remove the weakness. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project cautions that it protects only the traffic the system inspects and attacks variations its rules recognise. Arora calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures, or detection rules. He also highlights operational technology, systems that monitor or control physical processes such as energy, water and transport. Patching them can be difficult because downtime may affect safety or essential services.
title: AI’s ability to find cyber flaws outpacing firms’ capacity to fix them: Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora

enrich.summary_1line: Article argues smaller language models suit enterprise tasks needing tight evaluation, with LLMs used alongside them.

text:
As enterprises explore smaller language models for specialised tasks, developers see opportunities for tighter evaluation and control. But smaller models still

The push to deploy artificial intelligence across enterprise workflows has largely focused on increasingly capable large language models (LLMs). These systems generate content, interpret complex instructions, and power applications from customer support to software engineering. Yet as organisations move from experimentation to production, the priority shifts: the fundamental question is no longer just how capable a model is, but how reliably we can evaluate, govern, and control its behaviour. This dynamic is bringing smaller language models (SLMs) to the forefront. Purpose-built for targeted tasks and specific domains, SLMs handle discrete functions such as document processing, classification, information retrieval, and workflow automation. Instead of depending on a single, monolithic foundation model across an entire pipeline, enterprises can distribute tasks across architectures of varying sizes. However, industry experts caution against a common misconception: model size alone doesn't proxy for safety. “A smaller model is not automatically a safer model. Parameter count alone is not a safety guarantee,” says Anuj Gupta, founder and chief executive officer of KiteFishAI. “A poorly trained smaller model can be just as problematic within its intended application as a much larger model.” The core operational case for SLMs lies in scope definition. General-purpose LLMs are designed to handle an open-ended spectrum of user prompts, making it nearly impossible to anticipate every failure mode or edge case. Conversely, a specialised model operates within tightly defined parameters. “Smaller, specialised models can be easier to control because their capabilities and intended operating boundaries are more clearly defined,” Gupta explains. “When a model is trained for a specific domain or set of tasks, developers can build targeted evaluation datasets, test edge cases more extensively, and understand failure patterns more systematically.” Sourav Bandyopadhyay, founder and chief scientist at Shunya Labs, underscores that task-specific boundaries are vital for rigorous evaluation. “You can only evaluate what you can define. A general model's job is ‘anything’, so its test set is effectively infinite,” he notes. In contrast, when an SLM classifies customer requests into specific intent buckets, the challenge becomes a closed problem. Teams can curate a representative held-out test set, evaluate accuracy per class, and trace distinct failure mechanisms. Conventional academic benchmarks often fail to capture whether a system can execute a banking workflow, fetch proprietary records, or adhere to compliance policies. Building specialised pipelines addresses this disconnect. For instance, KiteFishAI is developing custom architectures and pretraining pipelines for document intelligence, workflow automation, and enterprise search across banking, financial services, and healthcare—though it has not yet publicly disclosed named client deployments or audited production metrics. Rather than outright displacing LLMs, organisations increasingly deploy SLMs alongside them in tiered architectures. In these setups, smaller models function as targeted verification and control layers. A high-capacity LLM can generate responses while dedicated SLMs validate outputs against retrieved context, filter sensitive information, or scan incoming queries for prompt injection. In agentic environments—where systems interact directly with databases and enterprise APIs—this separation of duties becomes critical. “Enterprises do not necessarily need to use one large model for every function,” Gupta says. “They can build a multi-model architecture where specialised smaller models act as independent control and verification layers.” Bandyopadhyay warns against letting decision-making models evaluate their own act
title: Smaller Language Models Could Reshape How Enterprises Deploy AI

text: The third quarter of 2026 offered an interesting insight into how AI is creating two different outcomes for the world’s largest digital advertising businesses. While Meta is using AI to improve ad targeting, recommendations, and campaign performance, Google faces a new challenge: monetising users who increasingly interact with its AI-powered search. In Q3, Meta reported advertising revenue of $63.06 billion, up 26% year-on-year. Google’s Search and other advertising revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion, down from 17% in the previous quarter and 19% in the first quarter. Surprisingly, Search accounted for less than 50% of Google revenue for the first time. Chatbots such as ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Meta’s new Muse assistant are becoming alternatives to traditional search. People ask these tools questions and get direct answers instead of clicking blue links on Google results pages. Fewer clicks mean fewer ad views and less revenue for Google. Google’s own AI features are also part of the shift. AI Overviews and AI Mode give users summaries and conversational answers. “The real shift is towards zero-click search. One AI conversation now does the work of five or six searches, and the user never lands on a results page where the ad lives. That is where the keyword model is exposed,” Viren Inaniyan, Co-founder and CEO of Tru Commerce, tells AIM. Google said AI Mode queries are, on average, three times longer than normal searches. Yet these AI experiences currently earn less money per query than traditional search. “Google has indicated that AI Mode currently monetises at a lower rate than traditional search. Part of this challenge is that most Google searches already end without a click, a pattern often called zero-click. AI Mode adds another dimension to this, as customers can now get more complete answers without needing to visit another page,” says Jacob Joseph, VP – Data Science, CleverTap Philipp Schindler, Google’s Chief Business Officer, said AI Mode’s lower monetisation contributed to the slowdown in Search revenue growth. The challenge is that AI-generated answers can satisfy users without requiring them to visit multiple websites or click through several search results. This could reduce opportunities for traditional sponsored links, particularly if users increasingly complete their research within AI interfaces. Schindler attributed the sequential slowdown in Search revenue growth primarily to foreign exchange movements, which he described as the single largest factor. Vertical-specific spending trends also weighed on growth, with retail advertisers in APAC affected by the EU’s elimination of its de minimis exemption, while media and entertainment spending normalised after a FIFA World Cup-driven surge in Q2. The question is whether Google earns more or less from the full journey, not per query,” he notes. Meta’s approach is different. text:
Security, governance and model dependence are emerging as major concerns for businesses, even as executives report productivity gains from AI investments.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) found that 84% of executives across enterprises identified productivity improvements as the leading benefit of AI investments. However, only 10% of enterprises allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple business functions. Only 9% of executives reported that their organisations had AI agents that could securely orchestrate workflows across enterprise applications. Security, risk and governance emerged as the leading considerations when organisations decide where and how to deploy AI systems. These factors ranked ahead of cost, speed and ease of deployment. Amit Kapur, Chief AI and Services Transformation Officer at TCS, said, “What seems to be holding organisations back – and rightly so – are concerns around security, governance, and resilience.” He added, “Deploying AI responsibly, with the right guardrails and enterprise controls, will be the big focus in the next stage of this journey.” As agents gain access to enterprise systems, observability becomes important for monitoring their actions and decisions. The study also found that 90% of respondents considered model independence an important factor in AI investment decisions. However, only 7% reported having organisation-wide continuity plans to switch AI providers. About 34% of respondents identified AI sovereignty requirements, including control over data location, model choice, and regulatory compliance, as a high or very high organisational risk. In Europe, the figure rose to 43%. Separately, legacy systems, fragmented data and integration gaps are emerging as obstacles to scaling AI deployments. A recent assessment of Indian enterprises highlighted infrastructure challenges in moving AI workloads into production, as organisations assess whether their existing infrastructure can support AI at scale. AI economics remain unsettled. Thirty-nine percent of enterprises said they were still assessing whether their AI initiatives generated sufficient value relative to token and compute costs. Fidelity International has introduced use-case-level token budgets and an internal AI gateway to monitor expenditure and restrict access. Its approach to managing AI costs and model access offers an example of how organisations are addressing these concerns. Meanwhile, 44% of respondents said important business knowledge remained embedded in employees' expertise or fragmented documentation, potentially limiting AI systems' access to enterprise context. Another 46% reported deploying open-source AI for selected use cases. The proportion of leaders who said it was too early to determine AI's effect on jobs rose from 4% in 2024 to 19% in 2026. North America showed particular strength across several enterprise AI foundations, with 15% of respondents treating AI as a strategic enterprise capability. The UK and Ireland reported comparatively higher levels of continuity planning and governance integration. The study, titled Intelligence that is Real, surveyed 1,333 senior business and technology leaders across 25 countries and 12 industries. Their organisations had annual revenues ranging from $500 million to more than $20 billion.
title: 84% See AI Productivity Gains, but Only 10% Allow Agent Autonomy: TCS Study

enrich.summary_1line: MIT CSAIL researchers report LLMs can read and edit neural network weights directly, without gradient-based training.

label.reason: MIT research on LLMs reading and editing neural network weights; interesting LLM research, not directly buildable.

text: Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) have shown that large language models (LLMs) can read, interpret, and modify neural network weights directly, without relying on traditional training methods like gradient descent. In a research blog post published on November 2, the researchers introduced a technique called Weight-Space Programming, which lets general-purpose LLMs examine a neural network’s weights, identify problems in its behaviour, and modify them based on natural-language instructions. The research was conducted by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, all affiliated with MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). The researchers used OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to demonstrate the approach across eight experiments, including identifying what a neural network was trained to do, writing networks from scratch and improving the mathematical reasoning capabilities of an existing language model. “We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we'd expect from humans or conventional algorithms,” the researchers wrote. One key experiment involved improving Qwen3.5-0.8B, a small language model, without retraining it or using gradient information. Astra identified a problem in the model’s weights that caused it to repeat reasoning steps instead of producing answers. By modifying just 0.016% of the model’s weights, Astra increased its score on the MATH-500 benchmark from 7.9% to 48.1%. Its score on GSM8K, another mathematical reasoning benchmark, increased from 13.8% to 67.1%. The researchers also found that the changes improved the model’s instruction-following performance. Its IFEval score increased from 21% to 62.3%. In the first set of experiments, the researchers tested whether Astra could identify a network’s behaviour by examining its weights without running the network. They trained four neural networks using Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) to play Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway. All four networks had the same architecture, input channels and possible actions. Astra received the 17,253 weights of each network as text, without being told which game it had been trained on. It correctly identified all four games. In another experiment, the researchers tested three diffusion models trained to generate circles, squares and triangles. Astra identified the shape each model generated by examining its weights, without running the models or performing forward passes. The researchers then tested whether an LLM could create neural networks without training them. They gave Astra the rules and source code for three MinAtar games: Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. enrich.summary_1line: Amazon memo tells engineers to measure long-term outcomes, not AI usage metrics such as token counts or tools used.

label.reason: Amazon memo on AI-powered engineering expectations; relevant to engineering careers and practices.

text: As concerns grow over AI’s impact on software engineering jobs, Amazon has issued a memo outlining what it expects from its engineers as AI reshapes software development. While acknowledging AI’s capabilities in software engineering and its long-term prospects, Amazon said, “It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI-powered engineering practices look like.” “Any definition we write now will likely look antiquated by this time next year,” the company added. And these ‘antiquated definitions’ risk slowing down progress, says Amazon, which wants to focus on what isn’t changing in software engineering roles. “Specifically, impact on our customers, our businesses, and our teams. The outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever,” said the company. The company said that metrics that often grab attention, such as token usage, the number of AI tools used, code changes, the number of reviews, and more, are “deeply flawed”. Amazon said that these metrics are “disconnected from what matters”. It adds that if teams use these metrics as targets—not just measurements—they could drive negative outcomes, increasing costs and complexity. “We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes. But these outcomes can be time-delayed, difficult to measure, and hard to isolate from other trends,” said the company. Amazon recommends that engineering teams use AI adoption metrics carefully, paying particular attention to the 10% of teams with the lowest adoption and the 10% with the highest adoption. The company wants managers to investigate why some teams struggle to incorporate AI into their workflows and whether teams using AI extensively deliver corresponding productivity improvements. Amazon said its most AI-forward teams have seen productivity and delivery improvements. It also warned that engineers and teams that don’t adopt AI or increase their output risk falling behind. However, the company said engineers shouldn’t be expected to use AI for every task. “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” Amazon said. It added that an engineer who can explain where AI falls short is demonstrating the judgement the company expects. Amazon also wants engineering leaders to gain hands-on experience with AI tools rather than relying on second-hand accounts of their capabilities. Managers should be able to identify tasks where AI has improved their teams’ work, as well as those where it has not, and explain the reasoning behind their decisions. Another priority is reconnecting engineers with customers and the businesses they serve. Amazon said some individual contributors and software development managers had become less connected to customers and business priorities as the company grew.
title: Amazon Warns Engineers Against AI Productivity Traps in Latest Memo

enrich.summary_1line: Article argues inference cost should be measured per completed task at agreed service levels, not by token or GPU prices alone.

label.reason: Production LLM serving economics: KV-cache pressure, latency, concurrency, cost; directly relevant to inference serving.

text: An AI model may prove its capabilities during evaluation, but the real test begins when users start using it at scale. A benchmark measures model capability under controlled conditions; production serving must meet latency, concurrency, availability and cost targets under variable demand. Long prompts increase prompt-processing demand; variable output lengths make capacity harder to predict; bursty traffic creates queues; and KV-cache pressure, replication for resilience, and idle capacity required for peak demand all raise the effective cost of serving each request. Inference is not a one-time compute event. It is a continuous production workload whose cost and performance depend on traffic patterns, response-time targets, model size, context length, concurrency, and the compute required to complete each task. Those economics also vary sharply by workload type: batch inference can prioritise throughput and scheduling flexibility, while interactive chat, voice, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic workflows and real-time decisioning have very different latency, availability and capacity requirements. That changes the economics of AI infrastructure. GPU hourly rates and API prices tell only part of the story. The real question is the cost per successful task at an agreed service level, measured by time-to-first-token, end-to-end latency, availability, quality and error rate. An important paradox lies at the heart of AI infrastructure. Inference has become dramatically cheaper, but the decline in token prices is not uniform across model classes, geographies, input and output tokens, or reserved and on-demand capacity. The cost of querying a model with GPT-3.5-level performance on the MMLU benchmark has fallen sharply. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index puts the price at $20 per million tokens in November 2022, compared with $0.07 per million tokens for Gemini 1.5 Flash-8B in October 2024, a more than 280-fold decline in about 18 months. The report also found that, across the models and tasks included in its analysis, the cost of inference fell by roughly nine to 900 times per year, depending on the task and model-performance level measured. This broader estimate refers to inference price reductions, rather than hardware efficiency or a uniform decline across production workloads. Lower unit prices have coincided with models being used for increasingly demanding workloads. Reasoning models can generate substantially more tokens, while agents can make multiple model calls, invoke tools and carry context from one step to the next. For example, a reasoning workflow may use a smaller number of requests but produce far more generated tokens and hold accelerator memory for longer. The result is that cost per token and cost per completed task are increasingly different metrics. A completed task could be a customer case resolved without escalation, a KYC document correctly classified, or a claims summary accepted by a reviewer. Even a nominally simple assistant may involve retrieval, safety checks and a generation model; an agent adds planning, repeated model calls, tool execution and retries. The unit price may be falling while the amount of inference required to complete a task is increasing. That is why production AI economics cannot stop at the API price sheet. This is particularly true when output tokens, context windows, retries and tool-call loops increase faster than the decline in unit price. It is useful for any inference system to measure how many requests it can complete, or how many tokens it can generate, while meeting the application’s quality and latency targets. Throughput complements latency: it shows how much work the system can complete while still meeting the latency target. Latency refers to how quickly an AI system can respond to an individual request, while throughput measures how much work it can handle within a given period, often expressed as requests or tokens per second across multiple users. title: The Economics of Continuous Inference

text:
In the new recommendation, TRAI has proposed a new authorisation category for satellite network providers which will allow them to supply network capacity directly to TSPs and recommends network control facilities to be located in India. The post TRAI recommends India-based network control, traffic monitoring for satellite providers appeared first on MEDIANAMA .

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) on November 5, 2026, released recommendations on a framework for Satellite Communication Network (SCN) provider authorisation and spectrum assignment. The recommendations propose a new authorisation category for satellite network providers, who would supply network capacity to eligible telecom service providers rather than directly serve users. Alongside the proposed framework, TRAI has set out security conditions governing network control, monitoring, gateway infrastructure and the use of satellite networks for cross-border services. Network Control Facilities Must Be Located in India: TRAI has recommended that the operation, maintenance and control facilities for an SCN provider’s satellite communication network be located in India. The requirement would also cover user terminals belonging to partnering authorised entities that connect to the provider’s network. SCN providers must ensure that their networks are used only to deliver telecommunications services for which the partnering entity holds authorisation. They must also prevent their networks from being used for unauthorised activities, including surveillance and electronic warfare, or in a manner that could prejudice India’s sovereignty and security. The recommendations further require SCN providers to report to the Central Government any attempt to access or use their satellite networks through a user terminal that is not registered with the partnering entity. The report must include information about the terminal and its location. To meet this requirement, providers must undertake the technical measures necessary to identify and report such attempts. However, TRAI has not prescribed a specific technology, protocol or authentication mechanism for detecting unregistered terminals. Government Can Direct Security Measures For Satellite Gateways: TRAI has proposed that SCN providers submit the location and technical details of each satellite earth station gateway to the Central Government or a designated agency before establishing it. The government or agency may examine the submitted information and direct the provider to take specific actions in relation to the gateway’s establishment. The recommendations also require SCN providers to furnish information and conduct interference-monitoring tests, as well as implement mitigation measures, as directed by the government. These provisions would give the government a role in reviewing gateway infrastructure before it is set up and in requiring operational measures where necessary. Separately, TRAI has recommended that SCN providers offer a real-time traffic monitoring facility to ensure compliance with requirements governing Indian user traffic. This includes restrictions on routing traffic through foreign gateways and on mirroring Indian traffic to foreign satellite or telecom networks. The recommendations also state that user terminals connected to a partnering authorised entity must not communicate directly through satellites without routing via a satellite earth station gateway. These conditions form part of the technical and operating obligations proposed for SCN provider authorisation.
